payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(primary source)
Letter urging renewed investment in a colony on the Roanoke coast
Letter from Edmund Rawcliffe, a fictional London cloth merchant who had invested in the 1585 voyage to Roanoke, to fellow merchants, early 1587 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Elizabethan promotional writing)

"Good sirs, I hear that some of the men lately come home from the island of Roanoke speak ill of that country, saying they found neither gold nor plenty and went hungry. I answer that they went hungry because they would rather dig for mines than plant corn, and because they quarreled with the very natives who first fed them. The soil there bears maize twice in a season, the woods yield cedar and sassafras, and the waters are thick with fish. Let us send families this time, and not soldiers only, so that they may till the ground and stay. Consider also that the King of Spain grows fat on the silver of the Indies and turns it against us and against the true religion. A settlement on that coast would furnish goods we now buy dear from strangers, set our idle poor to honest labor, and give our ships a harbor near his treasure fleets. I pray you, venture your purses once more."

ush_set.theme: Early English colonization attempts such as Roanoke
ush_set.title: A London Merchant Defends the Roanoke Venture, 1587

sources.title: Letter urging renewed investment in a colony on the Roanoke coast
sources.attribution: Letter from Edmund Rawcliffe, a fictional London cloth merchant who had invested in the 1585 voyage to Roanoke, to fellow merchants, early 1587 (ALTON-composed, in the style of Elizabethan promotional writing)

items.stem: Rawcliffe's purpose in writing the letter was most likely to

options.text: persuade investors to fund another colony despite reports of failure
options.why: Rawcliffe answers returned men who 'speak ill of that country' and closes by asking merchants to 'venture your purses once more,' matching the effort to fund a new Roanoke venture after Lane's colonists returned in 1586.
options.label: key

options.text: urge the crown to send soldiers to defend the settlers against attacks led by Powhatan's confederacy
options.why: The Powhatan confederacy's conflicts were with Jamestown after 1607, and Rawcliffe actually asks for families rather than only soldiers.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: petition the queen for a charter permitting dissenting Protestants to worship freely abroad
options.why: Seeking religious refuge drove later Separatist and Puritan settlement in the 1620s; the letter is addressed to merchants and is about profit and rivalry, not a petition for dissenters.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: announce to London merchants the discovery of gold and silver mines near the Roanoke settlement
options.why: The letter admits the colonists found no gold and criticizes them for hunting mines instead of planting.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "persuade investors to fund another colony despite reports of failure". Rawcliffe answers returned men who 'speak ill of that country' and closes by asking merchants to 'venture your purses once more,' matching the effort to fund a new Roanoke venture after Lane's colonists returned in 1586.
"urge the crown to send soldiers to defend the settlers against attacks led by Powhatan's confederacy" is incorrect: The Powhatan confederacy's conflicts were with Jamestown after 1607, and Rawcliffe actually asks for families rather than only soldiers.
"petition the queen for a charter permitting dissenting Protestants to worship freely abroad" is incorrect: Seeking religious refuge drove later Separatist and Puritan settlement in the 1620s; the letter is addressed to merchants and is about profit and rivalry, not a petition for dissenters.
"announce to London merchants the discovery of gold and silver mines near the Roanoke settlement" is incorrect: The letter admits the colonists found no gold and criticizes them for hunting mines instead of planting.
facts: Ralph Lane's Roanoke colonists, sent in 1585, abandoned the settlement and returned to England in 1586.
A new group including families sailed to Roanoke under John White in 1587.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Rawcliffe's explanation for the hardships suffered by the earlier Roanoke colonists?

options.text: The coast's poor soil and harsh climate made growing food impossible for any settlers
options.why: Rawcliffe praises the soil as bearing maize twice in a season, the opposite of this claim.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The settlers' own choices, such as seeking mines over farming, caused their hunger
options.why: Rawcliffe says the men went hungry because they 'would rather dig for mines than plant corn' and quarreled with the natives who fed them, which blames the colonists' conduct.
options.label: key

options.text: Native peoples refused all contact with the English from the moment the colonists first landed there
options.why: The letter says the natives 'first fed' the colonists before the English quarreled with them.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Spanish raids from Florida destroyed the colony's crops and supply ships before harvest
options.why: The letter mentions Spain only as a rival growing rich on silver, not as the cause of the colonists' hunger.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The settlers' own choices, such as seeking mines over farming, caused their hunger". Rawcliffe says the men went hungry because they 'would rather dig for mines than plant corn' and quarreled with the natives who fed them, which blames the colonists' conduct.
"The coast's poor soil and harsh climate made growing food impossible for any settlers" is incorrect: Rawcliffe praises the soil as bearing maize twice in a season, the opposite of this claim.
"Native peoples refused all contact with the English from the moment the colonists first landed there" is incorrect: The letter says the natives 'first fed' the colonists before the English quarreled with them.
"Spanish raids from Florida destroyed the colony's crops and supply ships before harvest" is incorrect: The letter mentions Spain only as a rival growing rich on silver, not as the cause of the colonists' hunger.
facts: The 1585-1586 Roanoke colonists depended heavily on food from the local Algonquian peoples, and relations broke down into violence.

items.stem: Rawcliffe's references to the King of Spain best reflect which broader context of the late 1500s?

options.text: Spain's alliance with England against France for control of the fur trade along the Saint Lawrence River
options.why: Spain and England were enemies in the 1580s, and the Saint Lawrence fur trade involved the French, not an Anglo-Spanish alliance.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: English acceptance of the Treaty of Tordesillas, which had granted England rights to North America's coast
options.why: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal and gave England nothing. England ignored it rather than accepting it.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Anglo-Spanish rivalry fueled by religious conflict and Spain's American silver
options.why: The letter links Spain's 'silver of the Indies' to hostility toward England and 'the true religion,' reflecting Protestant England's rivalry with Catholic Spain that led to war in 1585-1588.
options.label: key

options.text: Competition among European powers to control the Atlantic slave trade under the Navigation Acts
options.why: England's Navigation Acts began in 1651, well after this letter, and the letter does not discuss the slave trade.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Anglo-Spanish rivalry fueled by religious conflict and Spain's American silver". The letter links Spain's 'silver of the Indies' to hostility toward England and 'the true religion,' reflecting Protestant England's rivalry with Catholic Spain that led to war in 1585-1588.
"Spain's alliance with England against France for control of the fur trade along the Saint Lawrence River" is incorrect: Spain and England were enemies in the 1580s, and the Saint Lawrence fur trade involved the French, not an Anglo-Spanish alliance.
"English acceptance of the Treaty of Tordesillas, which had granted England rights to North America's coast" is incorrect: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal and gave England nothing. England ignored it rather than accepting it.
"Competition among European powers to control the Atlantic slave trade under the Navigation Acts" is incorrect: England's Navigation Acts began in 1651, well after this letter, and the letter does not discuss the slave trade.
facts: Spain drew enormous silver wealth from American mines such as Potosí in the 1500s.
Protestant England and Catholic Spain were rivals, leading to open war and the Spanish Armada's defeat in 1588.

items.stem: The colonizing venture Rawcliffe promotes was most similar to the English settlement at Jamestown, founded in 1607, in that both

options.text: were organized mainly to provide a refuge for Puritans seeking to purify the Church of England
options.why: Religious refuge for Puritans describes Massachusetts Bay (1630), not Roanoke or Jamestown, which aimed at profit and rivalry with Spain.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: depended on Native laborers forced to work under the encomienda system established by the English crown
options.why: The encomienda was a Spanish colonial labor system, not an English one.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: quickly achieved prosperity by exporting tobacco grown by enslaved Africans on large plantations
options.why: Roanoke never prospered. Jamestown's tobacco boom came after 1612 and relied mostly on indentured servants at first, so 'quickly' and 'enslaved Africans' are wrong for its early years.
options.label: overstated

options.text: relied on private investors and struggled at first to feed their settlers
options.why: Roanoke depended on private investors, as Rawcliffe's appeal to merchants shows, and its colonists went hungry. Jamestown was funded by the joint-stock Virginia Company and nearly collapsed from food shortages.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "relied on private investors and struggled at first to feed their settlers". Roanoke depended on private investors, as Rawcliffe's appeal to merchants shows, and its colonists went hungry. Jamestown was funded by the joint-stock Virginia Company and nearly collapsed from food shortages.
"were organized mainly to provide a refuge for Puritans seeking to purify the Church of England" is incorrect: Religious refuge for Puritans describes Massachusetts Bay (1630), not Roanoke or Jamestown, which aimed at profit and rivalry with Spain.
"depended on Native laborers forced to work under the encomienda system established by the English crown" is incorrect: The encomienda was a Spanish colonial labor system, not an English one.
"quickly achieved prosperity by exporting tobacco grown by enslaved Africans on large plantations" is incorrect: Roanoke never prospered. Jamestown's tobacco boom came after 1612 and relied mostly on indentured servants at first, so 'quickly' and 'enslaved Africans' are wrong for its early years.
facts: Jamestown was founded in 1607 by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company chartered in 1606.
Jamestown suffered severe food shortages in its early years, including the 'starving time' of 1609-1610.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
Excerpt on the origins of African bondage in the Iberian Americas
Marisol Ekwueme-Barros, historian, from the fictional book Salt, Sugar, and Sail: The Iberian Roots of Atlantic Bondage, published by a university press in Lisbon and Chicago, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern scholarly monograph)

"The Atlantic slave trade did not begin in the Americas; it was carried there. By the 1480s Portuguese captains at fortified posts along the Gold Coast were buying captives from African rulers and shipping them to sugar estates on Madeira and Sao Tome. Those island plantations served as a rehearsal. They joined European capital, African labor, and a single export crop under harsh discipline. When Spanish settlers on Hispaniola watched the Taino population collapse within a generation of 1492, they turned to this proven model. Royal licenses to import Africans soon followed, and the crown's later efforts to curb abuses of Native laborers only deepened colonists' reliance on African captives. By the end of the sixteenth century, the sugar mills of Portuguese Brazil had become the largest destination for enslaved Africans in the Americas. Bondage in the Iberian colonies, in short, was less an improvisation than the export of a system already tested in the eastern Atlantic."

facts: Portuguese colonists established sugar plantations on Madeira and Sao Tome in the fifteenth century using enslaved African labor.
The Portuguese built the fortified trading post of Elmina on the Gold Coast in 1482.

items.stem: The pattern of labor and production described in the excerpt is most similar to which of the following developments in the seventeenth century?

options.text: Puritan settlers in New England building towns around family farms, congregations, and local town meetings
options.why: New England's family-farm economy did not depend on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Spanish missionaries in New Mexico compelling Pueblo peoples to labor and convert, provoking the Pueblo Revolt of 1680

options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: English planters on Barbados turning to enslaved Africans to grow sugar for export
options.why: The Barbados sugar boom repeated the Iberian model the author describes: a single export crop, European capital, and enslaved African labor under harsh discipline.
options.label: key

The correct answer is "English planters on Barbados turning to enslaved Africans to grow sugar for export". The Barbados sugar boom repeated the Iberian model the author describes: a single export crop, European capital, and enslaved African labor under harsh discipline.
"Puritan settlers in New England building towns around family farms, congregations, and local town meetings" is incorrect: New England's family-farm economy did not depend on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
Source A (primary source)
Letter of a Dominican friar to the Council of the Indies
Fray Anselmo de Zárate, a fictional Dominican friar, writing from Antequera in the valley of Oaxaca to the Council of the Indies, 1549 (ALTON-composed, in the style of mid-sixteenth-century missionary letters)

"Most powerful lords, I have walked these valleys for eleven years, and I tell you the people here are not beasts, as some in Mexico claim. They keep markets more orderly than those of Seville, they choose officers to govern their towns, and their children learn the catechism faster than our own. Yet the holders of encomiendas drive them to the mines at Taxco and the sugar mills of the coast, and whole villages are left with only widows. How can a people love the Gospel when it comes to them with the overseer's whip? Faith must enter by persuasion and good example, never by force. I beg Your Lordships to enforce the new ordinances His Majesty has given, and to let no Spaniard hold Indians as his own."

———

Source B (primary source)
Petition of a town council in New Spain to the Crown
Petition signed by Hernando Villagómez, a fictional alderman, on behalf of the town council of a Spanish settlement in New Spain, addressed to the king, 1544 (ALTON-composed, in the style of colonial petitions against the New Laws)

"We who won this land at our own cost, with our own horses and arms, now learn that the new ordinances would take our encomiendas from our widows and sons. If this is done, the Spaniards will leave, and the Indians, left to themselves, will return to their idols and their idleness. It is the encomendero who builds the church in each town, pays the priest, and teaches the natives to work as Christians do. Without our labor and theirs, the mines will stand empty and Your Majesty's royal fifth will vanish. We ask only that the ordinances be suspended, so that this realm may remain both Christian and profitable."

options.text: Pueblo peoples in New Mexico rose up against Spanish missionaries and settlers in 1680 and drove them out for over a decade.

options.why: Silver wealth is real, but it fits Excerpt B's point about royal revenue better than the friar's claim that forced labor harms Native people.

options.label: true_but_not_responsive

The Pueblo Revolt took place in 1680.

items.stem: The debate shown in the two excerpts took place most directly in the context of

options.text: competition with English colonists who had set up profitable tobacco plantations around Jamestown in the Chesapeake
options.why: Jamestown was founded in 1607 and tobacco became its staple only later, decades after these excerpts were written.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Spanish and French rivalry over the fur trade and Native alliances in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence region
options.why: French fur-trading rivalries in the north had nothing to do with labor policy in New Spain in the 1540s.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: royal efforts to limit the power of conquistadors and encomenderos after Spain's conquest of the Aztec Empire
options.why: The Spanish Crown issued the New Laws in 1542 to restrict the encomienda and ban Native enslavement, partly to keep conquerors from becoming a hereditary nobility. The 'new ordinances' in both excerpts are these laws.
options.label: key

options.text: the spread of Enlightenment ideas about natural rights that challenged the divine authority of European monarchs
options.why: The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century movement. Both excerpts appeal to the king's authority and do not challenge it.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "royal efforts to limit the power of conquistadors and encomenderos after Spain's conquest of the Aztec Empire". The Spanish Crown issued the New Laws in 1542 to restrict the encomienda and ban Native enslavement, partly to keep conquerors from becoming a hereditary nobility. The 'new ordinances' in both excerpts are these laws.
"competition with English colonists who had set up profitable tobacco plantations around Jamestown in the Chesapeake" is incorrect: Jamestown was founded in 1607 and tobacco became its staple only later, decades after these excerpts were written.
"Spanish and French rivalry over the fur trade and Native alliances in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence region" is incorrect: French fur-trading rivalries in the north had nothing to do with labor policy in New Spain in the 1540s.
"the spread of Enlightenment ideas about natural rights that challenged the divine authority of European monarchs" is incorrect: The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century movement. Both excerpts appeal to the king's authority and do not challenge it.
facts: The Spanish Crown issued the New Laws in 1542, restricting the encomienda and prohibiting the enslavement of Native peoples.
Hernán Cortés and his Native allies conquered the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan in 1521.

items.stem: Spanish restrictions on Native enslavement, like those debated in the excerpts, most directly contributed to which development later in the sixteenth century?

options.text: English colonizers adopted the encomienda system to organize tobacco labor in early Virginia and Maryland
options.why: The encomienda was a Spanish institution. Chesapeake planters used indentured servants and later enslaved Africans.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: The Spanish Crown ended all forced Native labor and required colonists to pay Native workers market wages in every colony
options.why: Forced Native labor went on through the repartimiento and the mita in Peru. The Crown regulated coerced labor but did not abolish it.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Spanish authorities abandoned missionary work and allowed Native peoples to keep their own religious practices
options.why: Missionary efforts grew after the mid-1500s, and Spanish authorities kept suppressing Native religious practices.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Spanish colonists relied more and more on enslaved Africans as limits on Native enslavement grew
options.why: As the Crown restricted Native enslavement and Native populations declined, Spanish colonists imported more enslaved Africans. This helped the transatlantic slave trade grow.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Spanish colonists relied more and more on enslaved Africans as limits on Native enslavement grew". As the Crown restricted Native enslavement and Native populations declined, Spanish colonists imported more enslaved Africans. This helped the transatlantic slave trade grow.
"English colonizers adopted the encomienda system to organize tobacco labor in early Virginia and Maryland" is incorrect: The encomienda was a Spanish institution. Chesapeake planters used indentured servants and later enslaved Africans.
"The Spanish Crown ended all forced Native labor and required colonists to pay Native workers market wages in every colony" is incorrect: Forced Native labor went on through the repartimiento and the mita in Peru. The Crown regulated coerced labor but did not abolish it.
"Spanish authorities abandoned missionary work and allowed Native peoples to keep their own religious practices" is incorrect: Missionary efforts grew after the mid-1500s, and Spanish authorities kept suppressing Native religious practices.
facts: Spanish colonists increasingly imported enslaved Africans in the sixteenth century as Native populations declined and the Crown restricted Native enslavement.
Coerced Native labor continued in Spanish America through the repartimiento and the mita after the New Laws of 1542.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(primary source)
Letter from a Franciscan friar to the Council of the Indies
Fray Andrés de Valcárcel, a fictional Franciscan friar serving in a Native town in central New Spain, letter to the Council of the Indies in Spain, 1578 (ALTON-composed, in the style of sixteenth-century missionary reports)

"Most Powerful Lords: I write from the town of San Miguel Tecalco, where I have served the Indians for nineteen years. When I came, this valley held some four thousand households. After the great sickness of these two years past, I count fewer than nine hundred. The old men say their grandfathers knew no such pestilence before the Christians came, and I believe them, for the Spaniards of the town fall ill and most recover, while the natives die whole houses at once. Meanwhile the cattle and sheep of the estancias multiply beyond number. They break into the maize fields at night, and the few who remain cannot guard them. I beg Your Lordships to order the herds kept far from the Indian towns and to lighten the tribute and labor owed by the survivors, for the dead cannot pay, and the living are made to pay for them."

Letter from Nathaniel Pruett, a fictional deacon of the church at the fictional town of Hadleigh Falls, Massachusetts Bay Colony, to the elders of a neighboring church, 1660 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a seventeenth-century New England church letter)

"At our last town meeting, held in the meetinghouse the second Monday of March, the inhabitants voted forty pounds for our minister's maintenance and laid out the new lots beyond the mill brook. Yet I observed with grief how few at that meeting may stand as members of the church. Our fathers came into this wilderness to plant churches in covenant with God, and they gathered ours of those who could declare the work of grace upon their souls. Their sons now till the land, sit on the town's committees, and keep the Sabbath soberly, but most have never related any such experience before the congregation. Their children therefore go unbaptized. If the covenant be not opened to such persons, I fear that within one generation our church will be a small remnant amid a town of strangers to it, and this commonwealth will lose its godly foundation."

(secondary source)
Tobacco Planters and the Turn to Slave Labor
Miriam Halloway, historian, Leaf and Bond: Labor on the James and York Rivers, 1640-1720, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social history of the colonial Chesapeake)

"In the Chesapeake, slavery did not arrive as a finished system. Planters backed into it. For most of the seventeenth century, tobacco growers on the James and York Rivers preferred English servants bound for four to seven years, whose passage earned masters headrights to fifty acres of land. That preference eroded after 1660. Slower population growth and rising wages in England reduced the number of young men willing to sign indentures. Servants who outlived their terms crowded onto poor land and complained about taxes and frontier defense, grievances that exploded into armed revolt in 1676. When the Royal African Company lost its monopoly in 1698, independent traders brought far more captives into the Bay. Lawmakers, meanwhile, wrote the new order into statute, declaring in 1662 that a child's status followed that of its mother. By 1710, enslaved Africans had become the core of the field labor force. That outcome grew out of shifts in supply and price more than out of any single decision."

Address to the New Jersey Legislature on Gradual Emancipation
Address of the Freehold Township Friends of Liberty to the New Jersey legislature, drafted by Elias Vreeland, a Monmouth County farmer and Revolutionary War veteran, 1796 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a post-Revolutionary antislavery petition)

"Gentlemen, we who address you tilled our fields under the threat of British arms, and some of us carried muskets at Monmouth beside Black men who fought for a liberty they do not yet enjoy. The Declaration of our independence holds that all men are created equal and are endowed with a right to liberty. How can a state that bled for that principle still hold many thousands of persons in bondage? We do not ask you to strip any citizen of the servants he now holds, for we respect property lawfully acquired under our former laws. We ask only that every child hereafter born of an enslaved mother be declared free upon reaching mature years, after serving long enough to repay the cost of his rearing. Our neighbors across the Delaware adopted such a course sixteen years ago, and their commonwealth has suffered neither ruin nor disorder. Let New Jersey no longer lag behind her sister states in honoring the cause for which we fought."

ush_set.theme: Gradual abolition in Northern states after the Revolution
ush_set.title: A New Jersey Petition for Gradual Abolition, 1796

sources.title: Address to the New Jersey Legislature on Gradual Emancipation
sources.attribution: Address of the Freehold Township Friends of Liberty to the New Jersey legislature, drafted by Elias Vreeland, a Monmouth County farmer and Revolutionary War veteran, 1796 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a post-Revolutionary antislavery petition)

items.stem: The address's proposal that only children born after the law's passage be freed was most likely intended to

options.text: reassure slaveholding legislators that abolition would respect existing property rights
options.why: The authors say they will not strip any citizen of servants he now holds and that they respect lawfully acquired property. Gradual laws in the North were written this way to win over legislators who worried about slaveholders' losses.
options.label: key

options.text: win support for a plan to resettle freed Black children in a colony in West Africa once they came of age
options.why: The address says nothing about colonization. Organized colonization efforts such as the American Colonization Society came later, in 1816.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: persuade Congress to use its new constitutional authority to end the importation of enslaved Africans before 1808
options.why: The address is directed to a state legislature and concerns emancipation within the state. The Constitution also barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: satisfy Quaker reformers who demanded that all enslaved people in the state be freed at once without compensation
options.why: The address rejects immediate emancipation outright, and calls for immediate, uncompensated abolition came mainly in the 1830s.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "reassure slaveholding legislators that abolition would respect existing property rights". The authors say they will not strip any citizen of servants he now holds and that they respect lawfully acquired property. Gradual laws in the North were written this way to win over legislators who worried about slaveholders' losses.
"win support for a plan to resettle freed Black children in a colony in West Africa once they came of age" is incorrect: The address says nothing about colonization. Organized colonization efforts such as the American Colonization Society came later, in 1816.
"persuade Congress to use its new constitutional authority to end the importation of enslaved Africans before 1808" is incorrect: The address is directed to a state legislature and concerns emancipation within the state. The Constitution also barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808.
"satisfy Quaker reformers who demanded that all enslaved people in the state be freed at once without compensation" is incorrect: The address rejects immediate emancipation outright, and calls for immediate, uncompensated abolition came mainly in the 1830s.
facts: Northern gradual abolition laws, beginning with Pennsylvania's in 1780, typically freed only children born after passage and left those already enslaved in bondage.
The U.S. Constitution (1787) barred Congress from prohibiting the importation of enslaved people before 1808.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the authors' claim that a gradual plan would not ruin slaveholders?

options.text: The cotton gin, invented in 1793, made short-staple cotton profitable and sharply raised the market value of enslaved laborers in the Deep South
options.why: The cotton gin changed the Southern economy. It offers no evidence about how gradual emancipation affected Northern slaveholders.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Pennsylvania's 1780 act freed no one already enslaved and bound enslaved mothers' children to serve until 28
options.why: This shows that the 'neighbors across the Delaware' left owners' current labor force in place and gave them decades of service from children, which supports the claim that slaveholders suffered no ruin.
options.label: key

options.text: Massachusetts court rulings in the early 1780s held slavery incompatible with the state constitution's declaration of rights, ending it quickly
options.why: The Massachusetts rulings ended slavery quickly through the courts, not gradually. That is the opposite of a plan built to protect owners' existing property.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 barred slavery from the territory north of the Ohio River, where few slaveholders had yet settled with their laborers
options.why: The Ordinance is accurate, but it applied to a federal territory with few slaveholders. It says nothing about how a gradual plan affected owners in an established state.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Pennsylvania's 1780 act freed no one already enslaved and bound enslaved mothers' children to serve until 28". This shows that the 'neighbors across the Delaware' left owners' current labor force in place and gave them decades of service from children, which supports the claim that slaveholders suffered no ruin.
"The cotton gin, invented in 1793, made short-staple cotton profitable and sharply raised the market value of enslaved laborers in the Deep South" is incorrect: The cotton gin changed the Southern economy. It offers no evidence about how gradual emancipation affected Northern slaveholders.
"Massachusetts court rulings in the early 1780s held slavery incompatible with the state constitution's declaration of rights, ending it quickly" is incorrect: The Massachusetts rulings ended slavery quickly through the courts, not gradually. That is the opposite of a plan built to protect owners' existing property.
"The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 barred slavery from the territory north of the Ohio River, where few slaveholders had yet settled with their laborers" is incorrect: The Ordinance is accurate, but it applied to a federal territory with few slaveholders. It says nothing about how a gradual plan affected owners in an established state.
facts: Pennsylvania's Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery (1780) freed no one already enslaved, and children born to enslaved mothers after the act had to serve until age 28.
Massachusetts court decisions in the early 1780s (the Quock Walker cases) effectively ended slavery there under the 1780 state constitution.
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory.

items.stem: The address is best understood in the context of which broader development in the era of the American Revolution?

options.text: The new federal Constitution granted Congress authority to abolish slavery within any state that petitioned for national assistance
options.why: The Constitution gave Congress no power to abolish slavery inside the states. Abolition in the North came through state action, which is why the address goes to a state legislature.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Expanding factory production in New England created a demand for free wage labor that made slave ownership unprofitable in the North
options.why: Factory growth in New England belongs mainly to the Market Revolution after 1810. The address also makes an ideological case, not an economic one.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Revolutionary claims of natural rights led some Americans to question slavery and other inherited hierarchies
options.why: The address appeals to the Declaration and to wartime sacrifice. This fits the way Revolutionary ideals led to Northern abolition laws, more manumissions, and challenges to other hierarchies.
options.label: key

options.text: Evangelical revivals of the Second Great Awakening inspired reformers to demand the immediate, uncompensated emancipation of all enslaved people
options.why: The Second Great Awakening and immediatism came decades later, and the address calls for gradual emancipation, not immediate.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Revolutionary claims of natural rights led some Americans to question slavery and other inherited hierarchies". The address appeals to the Declaration and to wartime sacrifice. This fits the way Revolutionary ideals led to Northern abolition laws, more manumissions, and challenges to other hierarchies.
"The new federal Constitution granted Congress authority to abolish slavery within any state that petitioned for national assistance" is incorrect: The Constitution gave Congress no power to abolish slavery inside the states. Abolition in the North came through state action, which is why the address goes to a state legislature.
"Expanding factory production in New England created a demand for free wage labor that made slave ownership unprofitable in the North" is incorrect: Factory growth in New England belongs mainly to the Market Revolution after 1810. The address also makes an ideological case, not an economic one.
"Evangelical revivals of the Second Great Awakening inspired reformers to demand the immediate, uncompensated emancipation of all enslaved people" is incorrect: The Second Great Awakening and immediatism came decades later, and the address calls for gradual emancipation, not immediate.
facts: Revolutionary-era natural rights ideals, expressed in the Declaration of Independence (1776), led some Americans to challenge slavery and other inherited hierarchies.
The Second Great Awakening and immediatist abolitionism arose mainly in the early-to-mid nineteenth century, especially the 1820s and 1830s.

items.stem: Gradual abolition laws like the one proposed in the address contributed most directly to which development in the early 1800s?

options.text: Congressional abolition of the slave trade between states in 1808, which halted the sale of enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South
options.why: The 1808 ban covered only the international slave trade. The domestic trade from the Upper South to the Deep South grew after that.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which prohibited slavery in all federal territories and admitted Missouri as a free state alongside Maine
options.why: The Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It barred slavery only in the Louisiana Purchase lands north of 36 degrees 30 minutes.
options.label: overstated

options.text: The steady expansion of voting rights for free Black men in Northern states, which by the 1830s enjoyed suffrage on equal terms with whites
options.why: Northern states often restricted Black voting during this period. New York's 1821 constitution and Pennsylvania's 1838 constitution are examples, so this is the opposite of what happened.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The growth of free Black communities in Northern cities that founded their own churches and mutual aid societies
options.why: As gradual laws took effect, free Black populations grew in Northern cities and built independent institutions, such as the AME Church organized in Philadelphia in 1816.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The growth of free Black communities in Northern cities that founded their own churches and mutual aid societies". As gradual laws took effect, free Black populations grew in Northern cities and built independent institutions, such as the AME Church organized in Philadelphia in 1816.
"Congressional abolition of the slave trade between states in 1808, which halted the sale of enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South" is incorrect: The 1808 ban covered only the international slave trade. The domestic trade from the Upper South to the Deep South grew after that.
"The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which prohibited slavery in all federal territories and admitted Missouri as a free state alongside Maine" is incorrect: The Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It barred slavery only in the Louisiana Purchase lands north of 36 degrees 30 minutes.
"The steady expansion of voting rights for free Black men in Northern states, which by the 1830s enjoyed suffrage on equal terms with whites" is incorrect: Northern states often restricted Black voting during this period. New York's 1821 constitution and Pennsylvania's 1838 constitution are examples, so this is the opposite of what happened.
facts: Free Black communities in Northern cities grew in the early 1800s and founded independent institutions, including the African Methodist Episcopal Church, organized in Philadelphia in 1816.
Several Northern states restricted Black voting in the early 1800s, for example New York's 1821 constitution set a property requirement for Black men only.
The 1808 federal ban applied to the international slave trade; the interstate slave trade continued and grew.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
Choosing Sides in the Revolutionary Countryside
Excerpt from Hollis T. Wendover, Neighbors at Arms: Allegiance and Survival in the Revolutionary Countryside, a fictional study published in 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social historian of the American Revolution)

"Historians once sorted colonists neatly into Patriots and Loyalists, assuming each man chose his side after reading pamphlets on natural rights or weighing his ties to the Crown. The records of the war years tell a messier story. In the Carolina and New York backcountry, many families declared an allegiance only when an army or a militia company appeared at the door, and some changed sides more than once. Local committees of safety demanded oaths, disarmed suspected Tories, and seized their property, so that political loyalty became a question of survival. Old quarrels over land titles, debts, and church membership often decided which side a farmer took. For enslaved people, and for Native nations such as many of the Iroquois, the question was rarely abstract principle. It was which side seemed more likely to secure their freedom or their land. The Revolution was a war for independence, but it was also a civil war fought among neighbors."

ush_set.theme: Loyalists, Patriots and the experience of war
ush_set.title: Allegiance and Survival: The Revolution as a Civil War

sources.title: Choosing Sides in the Revolutionary Countryside
sources.attribution: Excerpt from Hollis T. Wendover, Neighbors at Arms: Allegiance and Survival in the Revolutionary Countryside, a fictional study published in 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a social historian of the American Revolution)

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?

options.text: Allegiance in the war often depended on local conditions and survival more than on political principle.
options.why: The author says choices came when armies arrived, under committee pressure, and from local quarrels, calling the war a civil war among neighbors.
options.label: key

options.text: Most colonists sided with the Patriots after Enlightenment ideas about natural rights convinced them that British rule was illegitimate.
options.why: The author rejects the older view that colonists picked sides after reading pamphlets on natural rights.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The war was fought mainly by professional armies, leaving most farm families in the backcountry largely untouched by the fighting.
options.why: The author stresses that the war reached backcountry homes directly through armies, militias, and committees.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Loyalists were chiefly royal officeholders and wealthy merchants whose commercial ties to Britain determined their political choices.
options.why: The excerpt focuses on backcountry farmers, enslaved people, and Native nations, not elite officeholders or merchants.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Allegiance in the war often depended on local conditions and survival more than on political principle.". The author says choices came when armies arrived, under committee pressure, and from local quarrels, calling the war a civil war among neighbors.
"Most colonists sided with the Patriots after Enlightenment ideas about natural rights convinced them that British rule was illegitimate." is incorrect: The author rejects the older view that colonists picked sides after reading pamphlets on natural rights.
"The war was fought mainly by professional armies, leaving most farm families in the backcountry largely untouched by the fighting." is incorrect: The author stresses that the war reached backcountry homes directly through armies, militias, and committees.
"Loyalists were chiefly royal officeholders and wealthy merchants whose commercial ties to Britain determined their political choices." is incorrect: The excerpt focuses on backcountry farmers, enslaved people, and Native nations, not elite officeholders or merchants.
facts: The American Revolution (1775-1783) divided colonists into Patriots, Loyalists, and many who tried to stay neutral.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support the author's claim that the Revolution was also a civil war fought among neighbors?

options.text: The siege of Yorktown in 1781 ended with the surrender of a British army to combined American and French forces under Washington.
options.why: Accurate, but it describes the defeat of a British army, not neighbors fighting neighbors.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: At Kings Mountain in 1780, nearly all the soldiers on both sides were American Patriot and Loyalist militiamen.
options.why: A major battle fought almost entirely between American militias on opposing sides directly shows colonists fighting one another.
options.label: key

options.text: France's 1778 alliance with the United States supplied troops, loans, and a navy that helped the Continental Army defeat Britain.
options.why: Accurate, but it concerns international aid against Britain, not conflict among colonists.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: Thomas Paine's Common Sense sold widely in 1776 and persuaded many readers that independence was justified by reason and nature.
options.why: Evidence that ideas persuaded colonists would challenge, not support, the author's emphasis on local and practical motives.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "At Kings Mountain in 1780, nearly all the soldiers on both sides were American Patriot and Loyalist militiamen.". A major battle fought almost entirely between American militias on opposing sides directly shows colonists fighting one another.
"The siege of Yorktown in 1781 ended with the surrender of a British army to combined American and French forces under Washington." is incorrect: Accurate, but it describes the defeat of a British army, not neighbors fighting neighbors.
"France's 1778 alliance with the United States supplied troops, loans, and a navy that helped the Continental Army defeat Britain." is incorrect: Accurate, but it concerns international aid against Britain, not conflict among colonists.
"Thomas Paine's Common Sense sold widely in 1776 and persuaded many readers that independence was justified by reason and nature." is incorrect: Evidence that ideas persuaded colonists would challenge, not support, the author's emphasis on local and practical motives.
facts: At the Battle of Kings Mountain in South Carolina in October 1780, Patriot militia defeated Loyalist militia; almost all combatants on both sides were Americans.
France formally allied with the United States in 1778.

items.stem: The choices of Native nations described in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 pledged that Native lands would never be taken without consent, leading Native nations to trust the new United States government.
options.why: The ordinance came after the war, so it could not shape wartime choices, and its promises did not earn lasting Native trust.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Spanish missions in New Mexico and California drew coastal and Pueblo peoples into labor systems that tied their survival to Catholic religious orders.
options.why: Spanish missions in the Southwest and Pacific coast had nothing to do with eastern Native nations' choices in the Revolution.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Many Native nations saw Britain as a check on settlers, since the Proclamation of 1763 had restricted settlement west of the Appalachians.
options.why: Because Britain had tried to limit westward settlement after 1763, many Native nations saw a British victory as the best way to protect their lands, which fits the excerpt's point about land.
options.label: key

options.text: The Iroquois Confederacy remained united behind the Patriot cause because the Albany Plan of Union had earlier tied the Six Nations to colonial governments.
options.why: The Iroquois split during the war, with most nations siding with Britain, and the Albany Plan was never adopted.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Many Native nations saw Britain as a check on settlers, since the Proclamation of 1763 had restricted settlement west of the Appalachians.". Because Britain had tried to limit westward settlement after 1763, many Native nations saw a British victory as the best way to protect their lands, which fits the excerpt's point about land.
"The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 pledged that Native lands would never be taken without consent, leading Native nations to trust the new United States government." is incorrect: The ordinance came after the war, so it could not shape wartime choices, and its promises did not earn lasting Native trust.
"Spanish missions in New Mexico and California drew coastal and Pueblo peoples into labor systems that tied their survival to Catholic religious orders." is incorrect: Spanish missions in the Southwest and Pacific coast had nothing to do with eastern Native nations' choices in the Revolution.
"The Iroquois Confederacy remained united behind the Patriot cause because the Albany Plan of Union had earlier tied the Six Nations to colonial governments." is incorrect: The Iroquois split during the war, with most nations siding with Britain, and the Albany Plan was never adopted.
facts: The Proclamation of 1763 restricted colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.
During the Revolution most Iroquois nations sided with Britain, although the Oneida and Tuscarora largely supported the Patriots.

items.stem: Which of the following was a direct result of the wartime treatment of suspected Loyalists described in the excerpt?

options.text: Former Loyalists became the core of the Federalist Party, using it to push for the return of confiscated property.
options.why: The Federalists formed in the 1790s around Hamilton's program; former Loyalists were not the party's base.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798 chiefly to punish former Loyalists who had kept their property after the war.
options.why: The acts targeted immigrants and Democratic-Republican critics of the Adams administration, not former Loyalists.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Shays' Rebellion in 1786 was led by dispossessed Loyalists demanding that Massachusetts return their confiscated farms.
options.why: The rebels were indebted farmers, many of them Patriot veterans, protesting taxes and foreclosures.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Tens of thousands of Loyalists left the United States, many of them resettling in British Canada.
options.why: Facing oaths, disarmament, and confiscated property, large numbers of Loyalists left, many for British North America.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Tens of thousands of Loyalists left the United States, many of them resettling in British Canada.". Facing oaths, disarmament, and confiscated property, large numbers of Loyalists left, many for British North America.
"Former Loyalists became the core of the Federalist Party, using it to push for the return of confiscated property." is incorrect: The Federalists formed in the 1790s around Hamilton's program; former Loyalists were not the party's base.
"Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798 chiefly to punish former Loyalists who had kept their property after the war." is incorrect: The acts targeted immigrants and Democratic-Republican critics of the Adams administration, not former Loyalists.
"Shays' Rebellion in 1786 was led by dispossessed Loyalists demanding that Massachusetts return their confiscated farms." is incorrect: The rebels were indebted farmers, many of them Patriot veterans, protesting taxes and foreclosures.
facts: During and after the Revolution, roughly 60,000 or more Loyalists left the United States, many settling in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec.
The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) targeted immigrants and critics of the Adams administration.
Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) was led by indebted western Massachusetts farmers, many of them Revolutionary War veterans.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
A historian reassesses the Jay Treaty
Clement Arvidson-Pryor, a fictional historian, in The Price of Quiet: Neutrality and Party in the Federalist Decade, a published lecture first delivered to the fictional Tidewater Historical Society, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern diplomatic historian)

"Crowds in 1795 burned John Jay in effigy, and it is tempting to read the treaty that bears his name as a surrender. That reading misses what the Washington administration was trying to buy. The president had already declared in 1793 that the United States would take no side in the war between Britain and France. When Jay sailed for London the next year, he carried little leverage. The nation had no navy worth the name, and most federal revenue came from import duties, the bulk of them collected on British goods. Measured against those weaknesses, the bargain looks rational. Britain promised to give up the forts it still held in the Northwest, and war with the strongest sea power was avoided. Yet Jay won nothing on the seizure of American sailors, and the price at home was steep. Protest meetings spread from Boston to Charleston, and the ratification fight turned a loose quarrel over policy into rival party organizations. Neutrality kept the republic out of Europe's war; it did not keep Europe's war out of American politics."

ush_set.theme: Washington's neutrality policy and the Jay Treaty
ush_set.title: Neutrality, the Jay Treaty, and the Price of Peace

sources.title: A historian reassesses the Jay Treaty
sources.attribution: Clement Arvidson-Pryor, a fictional historian, in The Price of Quiet: Neutrality and Party in the Federalist Decade, a published lecture first delivered to the fictional Tidewater Historical Society, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern diplomatic historian)

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: A treaty that disappointed many Americans was a reasonable bargain for a weak nation, but it intensified partisan conflict.
options.why: The author rejects the surrender reading, calls the bargain rational given American weakness, and says the ratification fight hardened rival party organizations.
options.label: key

options.text: The treaty was a humiliating capitulation to British demands that gained the United States nothing it had sought in negotiations.
options.why: The author mentions this view only to reject it, pointing to the promised evacuation of the Northwest forts and the avoidance of war.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Washington's neutrality policy successfully kept disputes over the European war from shaping American domestic politics in the 1790s.
options.why: The closing sentence says the opposite: neutrality did not keep Europe's war out of American politics.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Jay's mission succeeded chiefly because he persuaded British officials to stop seizing American sailors and forcing them into Royal Navy service.
options.why: The author states that Jay won nothing on impressment, and historically the treaty left impressment unresolved.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "A treaty that disappointed many Americans was a reasonable bargain for a weak nation, but it intensified partisan conflict.". The author rejects the surrender reading, calls the bargain rational given American weakness, and says the ratification fight hardened rival party organizations.
"The treaty was a humiliating capitulation to British demands that gained the United States nothing it had sought in negotiations." is incorrect: The author mentions this view only to reject it, pointing to the promised evacuation of the Northwest forts and the avoidance of war.
"Washington's neutrality policy successfully kept disputes over the European war from shaping American domestic politics in the 1790s." is incorrect: The closing sentence says the opposite: neutrality did not keep Europe's war out of American politics.
"Jay's mission succeeded chiefly because he persuaded British officials to stop seizing American sailors and forcing them into Royal Navy service." is incorrect: The author states that Jay won nothing on impressment, and historically the treaty left impressment unresolved.
facts: The Jay Treaty was negotiated in 1794 and approved by the Senate in 1795 amid widespread public protest.
Under the Jay Treaty, Britain agreed to evacuate its posts in the Northwest Territory, which it did in 1796.
The Jay Treaty did not end British impressment of American sailors.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the author's claim that the Jay Treaty was a rational bargain that improved the United States' position?

options.text: The continued British impressment of American sailors in the 1800s, which became a leading grievance behind the War of 1812.
options.why: Continued impressment points to the treaty's limits and would weaken the claim that it improved the nation's position.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Spain, fearing closer Anglo-American ties, granted Americans use of the Mississippi and New Orleans in 1795.
options.why: Pinckney's Treaty followed partly from Spanish worry over the Anglo-American agreement, so it shows the Jay Treaty strengthening the American position, as the author argues.
options.label: key

options.text: The XYZ Affair of 1797-1798, in which French agents demanded bribes from American diplomats before negotiations could begin.
options.why: The XYZ Affair came out of French anger at American policy and points to the treaty's costs, so it does not support the claim that the bargain improved the nation's position.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: The Washington administration's use of militia to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania in 1794.
options.why: The Whiskey Rebellion was about federal excise taxes and federal authority at home, not the results of diplomacy with Britain.
options.label: unrelated_development

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Spain, fearing closer Anglo-American ties, granted Americans use of the Mississippi and New Orleans in 1795.". Pinckney's Treaty followed partly from Spanish worry over the Anglo-American agreement, so it shows the Jay Treaty strengthening the American position, as the author argues.
"The continued British impressment of American sailors in the 1800s, which became a leading grievance behind the War of 1812." is incorrect: Continued impressment points to the treaty's limits and would weaken the claim that it improved the nation's position.
"The XYZ Affair of 1797-1798, in which French agents demanded bribes from American diplomats before negotiations could begin." is incorrect: The XYZ Affair came out of French anger at American policy and points to the treaty's costs, so it does not support the claim that the bargain improved the nation's position.
"The Washington administration's use of militia to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania in 1794." is incorrect: The Whiskey Rebellion was about federal excise taxes and federal authority at home, not the results of diplomacy with Britain.
facts: Pinckney's Treaty (Treaty of San Lorenzo) of 1795 gave Americans navigation of the Mississippi River and the right of deposit at New Orleans.
Spanish concern about closer Anglo-American relations after the Jay Treaty helped lead Spain to agree to Pinckney's Treaty in 1795.

items.stem: Which of the following provides the most direct context for the 1793 neutrality policy mentioned in the excerpt?

options.text: Napoleon's Continental System and the British Orders in Council, which together restricted neutral American shipping
options.why: These measures date from 1806-1807 and form the context for Jefferson's Embargo Act, not the 1793 proclamation.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Spain's closing of the lower Mississippi River to American traders in 1784, which angered western settlers
options.why: This happened, but it relates to Spanish-American relations and Pinckney's Treaty, not to the decision to stay out of the Anglo-French war.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: War between Britain and revolutionary France, which raised questions about the 1778 alliance with France
options.why: The 1793 war between Britain and France, along with the existing 1778 alliance, pushed Washington to declare that the United States would take no side.
options.label: key

options.text: Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts, which convinced many leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak
options.why: Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) shaped the move toward the Constitution, not foreign policy toward the European war.
options.label: unrelated_development

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "War between Britain and revolutionary France, which raised questions about the 1778 alliance with France". The 1793 war between Britain and France, along with the existing 1778 alliance, pushed Washington to declare that the United States would take no side.
"Napoleon's Continental System and the British Orders in Council, which together restricted neutral American shipping" is incorrect: These measures date from 1806-1807 and form the context for Jefferson's Embargo Act, not the 1793 proclamation.
"Spain's closing of the lower Mississippi River to American traders in 1784, which angered western settlers" is incorrect: This happened, but it relates to Spanish-American relations and Pinckney's Treaty, not to the decision to stay out of the Anglo-French war.
"Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts, which convinced many leaders that the Articles of Confederation were too weak" is incorrect: Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) shaped the move toward the Constitution, not foreign policy toward the European war.
facts: France declared war on Great Britain in February 1793 during the French Revolutionary Wars.
Washington issued the Neutrality Proclamation in April 1793.
The United States and France signed a Treaty of Alliance in 1778.

items.stem: The approach to foreign affairs that the excerpt attributes to the Washington administration was most consistent with which later development?

options.text: The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which restricted immigrants and criticism of the government during the Quasi-War
options.why: These were domestic security laws about dissent and immigration, not a continuation of a nonentanglement foreign policy.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: The declaration of war against Britain in 1812 after War Hawks demanded action over impressment and frontier raids
options.why: Going to war with Britain broke from the policy of avoiding war with the strongest sea power that the excerpt describes.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The Treaty of Alliance of 1778, which bound the United States and France together in a military partnership against Britain
options.why: The 1778 alliance came before the neutrality policy, not after it, and it was an entangling alliance, the opposite of neutrality.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The Monroe Doctrine's 1823 pledge that the United States would stay out of European wars
options.why: Like Washington's neutrality, the Monroe Doctrine kept the United States out of European conflicts, which continues the pattern of avoiding entanglement.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:

"I served four campaigns against the French and their Indian allies, and was promised, as were all who enlisted under the governor's proclamation of 1754, a share of lands upon the Ohio. Now word comes from London that the King has drawn a line along the heads of the rivers, and that no subject may settle or survey beyond it. We are told this is to quiet the Indians after the late troubles at Detroit and Fort Pitt. But who bled to clear that country? Not the ministers at Whitehall. Ten thousand regulars are to remain among us, and Parliament now speaks of a stamp duty to support them. So we are to be taxed for an army that keeps us out of the very lands our blood purchased. I cannot think the Crown means to treat its American subjects as tenants rather than as Englishmen."

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
Truces Between Rival Interests
Historian Marian Tollefsen, The Bargained Republic: Interest and Principle in Philadelphia, a study prepared for a seminar series at the fictional Harrow Valley Historical Society, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)

"Delegates who arrived in Philadelphia in May 1787 agreed that the Articles of Confederation had failed, but they agreed on little else. The bargains that followed are often remembered as triumphs of statesmanship, yet they are better understood as truces between rival interests. The Connecticut plan, which gave each state an equal vote in the Senate and apportioned the House by population, ended weeks of deadlock only after small-state delegates made clear they would reject any plan that denied them equal standing. Southern delegates secured the counting of three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and direct taxes, along with a clause barring Congress from ending the Atlantic slave trade before 1808. In return, New England delegates won a simple majority for laws regulating commerce rather than the two-thirds vote southerners had sought. Each settlement protected a particular constituency, and each postponed rather than resolved the questions of power that divided the states."

items.stem: The three-fifths clause described in the excerpt most directly affected national politics in the early 1800s in which of the following ways?

options.text: It drove New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention of 1814 to demand the immediate abolition of slavery throughout the South
options.why: The Hartford Convention proposed ending the three-fifths clause for representation, but it did not demand abolition of slavery in the South.
options.label: overstated

options.text: It granted free and enslaved African American men in southern states the right to vote in elections for the House
options.why: The clause counted enslaved people for apportionment without giving them any political rights; voting rules were left to the states.
options.label: reversal

options.text: It prompted the Confederation Congress to ban slavery north of the Ohio River through the Northwest Ordinance of 1787

options.label: misattributed

options.text: It enlarged the South's share of House seats and electoral votes, adding to slaveholding states' national influence
options.why: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people increased southern representation in the House and therefore in the Electoral College, strengthening slaveholding states in early national politics.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "It enlarged the South's share of House seats and electoral votes, adding to slaveholding states' national influence". Counting three-fifths of enslaved people increased southern representation in the House and therefore in the Electoral College, strengthening slaveholding states in early national politics.
"It drove New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention of 1814 to demand the immediate abolition of slavery throughout the South" is incorrect: The Hartford Convention proposed ending the three-fifths clause for representation, but it did not demand abolition of slavery in the South.
"It granted free and enslaved African American men in southern states the right to vote in elections for the House" is incorrect: The clause counted enslaved people for apportionment without giving them any political rights; voting rules were left to the states.
"It prompted the Confederation Congress to ban slavery north of the Ohio River through the Northwest Ordinance of 1787" is incorrect: The Northwest Ordinance was passed by the Confederation Congress in July 1787 independently of the Convention's three-fifths clause.
facts: The three-fifths clause of the Constitution (1787) counted three-fifths of enslaved people for apportionment of House seats and direct taxes.
Because each state's electoral votes equal its House seats plus its two Senate seats, the three-fifths clause also increased southern electoral votes.
The Hartford Convention (1814-1815) proposed constitutional amendments including ending the three-fifths clause for representation.

payload.set_intro:

(primary source)
Letter to the Freeholders of Amelia County
Ezra Whitlock, a fictional planter and former militia captain, in a printed letter to the voters of Amelia County, Virginia, 1791 (ALTON-composed, in the style of an Anti-Federalist and early Republican address to constituents)

"Friends and neighbors: When our soldiers came home from the late war, they were paid in certificates, and many sold those papers for a few shillings on the pound to keep their families fed. Now the Secretary of the Treasury would have Congress redeem these papers at their full face value, so that the gentlemen of Philadelphia and New York who bought them up may grow rich on the labor of the men who earned them. Nor is this all. Virginia has paid down much of her own war debt, yet we are to be taxed to pay the debts of states that paid little. And now a national bank is chartered, though I search the Constitution in vain for any power to create a corporation. If Congress may do whatever it deems useful, the states are nothing, and the planter and the farmer will be ruled by a moneyed few."

items.stem: Whitlock's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: A belief that close commercial ties with Great Britain were essential to restoring American credit abroad
options.why: Wanting close trade ties with Britain to restore credit was a Federalist position tied to Hamilton. Whitlock is attacking that program, not defending it.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Support for a loose interpretation of the Constitution that would let Congress fund roads and canals
options.why: Whitlock reads the Constitution strictly and rejects implied powers ('I search the Constitution in vain'). Loose construction is the view he opposes.

"Fear that the British would continue occupying forts in the Northwest Territory, threatening frontier settlers" is incorrect: British troops did stay in the northwestern forts until Jay's Treaty, but the excerpt is about finance and the Constitution, not frontier security.

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the author's claim about who would profit from redeeming the war certificates at full value?

options.text: Testimony that most original holders still kept their certificates and would receive full payment from the Treasury

"Testimony that most original holders still kept their certificates and would receive full payment from the Treasury" is incorrect: If the original holders still had their certificates, they would get the profit, not speculators. This would refute the author's claim.
"Reports that the Bank of the United States expanded credit and steadied the value of paper currency in commercial cities" is incorrect: This is about how the bank performed, not about who owned the certificates. If anything, it weakens the author's case against the bank.

items.stem: The arguments in the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following broader developments?

(secondary source)
The Crisis of 1798 and the Problem of Opposition
Historian Corinne Haldane Voss, from the published Wexford Lectures on the Early Republic, delivered at Linton College, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's interpretive lecture)

"We usually tell the story of 1798 as a clash between liberty and repression, but the deeper conflict was over whether an organized opposition could exist at all. Federalists in Congress, alarmed by the XYZ Affair and the undeclared naval war with France, lengthened the residency requirement for citizenship to fourteen years. They allowed the president to deport aliens he judged dangerous, and they made it a crime to publish false, scandalous, and malicious writing against the government. Nearly every prosecution under the Sedition Act fell on Republican printers or politicians, among them the Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon. The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, drafted in secret by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, replied that the laws were unconstitutional and that states could judge federal overreach. No other state legislature endorsed them. The Republicans won their real victory at the ballot box in 1800, yet the constitutional theory they had advanced outlived the party quarrel that produced it."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument of the excerpt?

items.stem: Which of the following facts would most directly support the excerpt's argument that the Sedition Act served Federalist partisan purposes?

options.label: key

options.why: This is true and shows how much the 1798 law lengthened residency, but it says nothing about the Sedition Act targeting the Republican opposition.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: Washington's Farewell Address of 1796 warned Americans against the dangers of a spirit of faction.

items.stem: The conflict described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development of the 1790s?

options.text: Federalist and Antifederalist arguments in state conventions over ratifying the new Constitution in 1788

items.stem: The constitutional theory advanced in the resolutions, as described in the excerpt, most directly anticipated which later development in the first half of the 1800s?

options.text: The Missouri Compromise of 1820, which admitted Maine and Missouri together to preserve the sectional balance in the Senate
options.why: The Missouri Compromise was a congressional settlement over slavery's expansion. It did not assert that a state could declare federal law void.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: The Supreme Court's ruling in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) that states could not tax a national bank
options.why: McCulloch affirmed federal supremacy over the states, which is the opposite of the state authority the resolutions claimed.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The Supreme Court's assertion in Marbury v. Madison (1803) of its power to strike down federal laws
options.why: Marbury placed the power to judge constitutionality in the federal courts, not in the states, so it does not continue the resolutions' claim.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: South Carolina's declaration in 1832 that federal tariff laws were void within the state
options.why: South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification of 1832 relied on the compact theory of the 1798 resolutions, which held that states could judge whether federal laws were constitutional.
options.label: key

Source A (secondary source)
Excerpt A: Corinne Valcourt on French aid
Corinne Valcourt, fictional historian, Bourbon Coin, Republican Victory, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic and military history of the Revolution)

"Without the alliance signed in February 1778, the American cause would probably have stalled into an exhausting stalemate. French loans and gifts kept the Continental Army clothed and armed after Congress's paper money had nearly collapsed. More decisively, French sea power changed the geography of the war. In the autumn of 1781, a French fleet held the mouth of the Chesapeake while French and American troops tightened the siege at Yorktown, leaving the British army there with no escape by water. The surrender that followed persuaded Parliament to give up offensive war in America. Independence was won on American soil, but a Bourbon king's treasury and navy made it possible."

———

Source B (secondary source)
Excerpt B: Desmond Hallorann on the peace negotiations
Desmond Hallorann, fictional historian, The Commissioners' Gamble: Americans at the Paris Peace, 2004 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a history of early American diplomacy)

"Historians who credit France with American independence tend to end the story at Yorktown. Yet a military victory did not settle the shape of the peace. The French court had its own aims, including obligations to its Spanish ally, and it showed little interest in an American republic stretching to the Mississippi. Congress had instructed its commissioners in Paris to act only with French knowledge and advice. In 1782 they quietly set those instructions aside and bargained directly with British envoys. The result was a treaty in 1783 that granted not only independence but a western boundary at the Mississippi River and access to the Newfoundland fisheries, terms more generous than France would have pressed for."

items.stem: France's decision to ally with the United States in 1778, described in Excerpt A, is best understood in the context of

options.label: wrong_period

items.stem: The alliance described in both excerpts was most directly connected to which of the following later developments in the 1790s?

Memorial of the Farmers and Mechanics of Elk Prairie, Indiana
Petition sent to the United States Congress by residents of the fictional town of Elk Prairie, Indiana, December 1829 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a western petition to Congress)

"To the Honorable the Senate and House of Representatives: The undersigned farmers, millers, and mechanics of Elk Prairie respectfully represent that the produce of our fields finds no market worth the name. A barrel of flour that brings five dollars at Baltimore fetches scarcely two at our landing. The difference goes to the wagoner and to the long, dangerous passage by flatboat to New Orleans. The great canal of New York has shown what one work of internal improvement can do, for the farmers of that state's western counties now sell their grain at prices close to those of the seaboard. We therefore pray that Congress carry the Cumberland Road westward across our state and lend its aid to the proposed canal joining the Wabash to Lake Erie. We ask no favor for one section alone. The Pittsburgh manufacturer, protected by the tariff, will buy our pork and wheat, and we will buy his iron and glass. In this way the Union will be bound together by interest as well as by affection."

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the memorial?

options.text: To persuade Congress that federally funded transportation would tie western farms to national markets
options.why: The petitioners ask Congress to extend the Cumberland Road and aid a Wabash-Lake Erie canal so that their crops can reach markets at better prices. This reflects western interest in federal internal improvements in the 1820s.
