payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(primary source)
Address to a civil service reform club
Address by Ephraim T. Haskell, secretary of the Hartwell Civil Service Reform Club, to the club's members, Hartwell, Connecticut, February 1883 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age reform club address)

"Gentlemen, the bill is law. For the first time since the days of Jackson, a young man may enter the service of the United States by proving his fitness in an open examination rather than by carrying a ward boss's letter. A clerk in our own post office told me he paid two percent of his wages each autumn to the party committee, and he knew his desk would go to another man if he refused. Every change of administration brought a swarm of applicants to Washington, and the President spent his days parceling out offices like the spoils of a conquered town. The tragedy of the summer before last showed the nation where that road ends. Yet let no member mistake this act for a complete victory. The commission it creates reaches only a small portion of the offices; the rest remain the property of whichever party holds power. Our work is to see the classified list extended, office by office, until merit is the rule."

ush_set.theme: Pendleton Civil Service Act and Gilded Age politics
ush_set.title: A Reform Club Greets the Pendleton Act, 1883

sources.title: Address to a civil service reform club
sources.attribution: Address by Ephraim T. Haskell, secretary of the Hartwell Civil Service Reform Club, to the club's members, Hartwell, Connecticut, February 1883 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a Gilded Age reform club address)

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of Haskell's address?

options.text: To urge reformers to keep pressing for merit hiring in more federal offices
options.why: Haskell welcomes the new law but warns it is not a complete victory and calls for extending the classified list office by office. That is the goal of Gilded Age civil service reformers after 1883.
options.label: key

options.text: To ask Congress to regulate railroad rates, since monopolies had captured the state legislatures
options.why: Railroad regulation was a separate Gilded Age reform cause, and the excerpt never mentions it.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: To recruit postal clerks into a national labor union seeking higher wages and an eight-hour day
options.why: The post office clerk is mentioned only as an example of party assessments. The address is about how offices are filled, not about labor organizing.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: To call for repeal of the new law because it weakens the party organizations that mobilize voters
options.why: Haskell praises the law and attacks party patronage. Defending the parties was the position of spoilsmen, not reformers.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "To urge reformers to keep pressing for merit hiring in more federal offices". Haskell welcomes the new law but warns it is not a complete victory and calls for extending the classified list office by office. That is the goal of Gilded Age civil service reformers after 1883.
"To ask Congress to regulate railroad rates, since monopolies had captured the state legislatures" is incorrect: Railroad regulation was a separate Gilded Age reform cause, and the excerpt never mentions it.
"To recruit postal clerks into a national labor union seeking higher wages and an eight-hour day" is incorrect: The post office clerk is mentioned only as an example of party assessments. The address is about how offices are filled, not about labor organizing.
"To call for repeal of the new law because it weakens the party organizations that mobilize voters" is incorrect: Haskell praises the law and attacks party patronage. Defending the parties was the position of spoilsmen, not reformers.
facts: The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, signed in January 1883, created a Civil Service Commission and required competitive examinations for classified federal positions.
At first the Pendleton Act covered only a small share of federal jobs (about 10 percent), and later presidents expanded the classified list.

items.stem: Which of the following provided the most immediate context for the passage of the law that Haskell celebrates?

options.text: The disputed presidential election of 1876 and the bargain that ended federal military support for Reconstruction governments
options.why: The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed election and ended Reconstruction. It came years before the law and did not set off merit reform.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The Panic of 1873 and the long wave of railroad bankruptcies and unemployment that followed in its wake
options.why: The depression of the 1870s shaped labor and monetary politics. It was not the event that pushed Congress to pass civil service reform.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: The 1881 assassination of President James Garfield by a disappointed seeker of federal office
options.why: Speaking in early 1883, Haskell calls it 'the tragedy of the summer before last,' which points to Garfield's shooting in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker. The killing built public support for the Pendleton Act.
options.label: key

options.text: The impeachment of President Andrew Johnson in 1868 after he removed his secretary of war in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act
options.why: Johnson's impeachment came out of Reconstruction conflicts about fifteen years earlier. It was not the immediate background to civil service reform in 1883.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The 1881 assassination of President James Garfield by a disappointed seeker of federal office". Speaking in early 1883, Haskell calls it 'the tragedy of the summer before last,' which points to Garfield's shooting in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker. The killing built public support for the Pendleton Act.
"The disputed presidential election of 1876 and the bargain that ended federal military support for Reconstruction governments" is incorrect: The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed election and ended Reconstruction. It came years before the law and did not set off merit reform.
"The Panic of 1873 and the long wave of railroad bankruptcies and unemployment that followed in its wake" is incorrect: The depression of the 1870s shaped labor and monetary politics. It was not the event that pushed Congress to pass civil service reform.
"The impeachment of President Andrew Johnson in 1868 after he removed his secretary of war in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act" is incorrect: Johnson's impeachment came out of Reconstruction conflicts about fifteen years earlier. It was not the immediate background to civil service reform in 1883.
facts: President James A. Garfield was shot in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker, and died in September 1881.
Garfield's assassination strengthened public support for the Pendleton Act of 1883.

items.stem: Which of the following was a significant effect of the type of law described in the excerpt on national politics in the decades after 1883?

options.text: Voter turnout in national elections fell sharply in the 1880s because patronage no longer drew partisans to the polls
options.why: Turnout in presidential elections stayed very high through the 1880s and 1890s. Strong party loyalty remained a defining feature of Gilded Age politics.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Federal employees won the right to bargain collectively and to strike against the national government
options.why: The law set up merit hiring and protections, not collective bargaining. Federal workers gained no right to strike in this period.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: Party machines in large cities collapsed as municipal jobs became subject to federal competitive examinations
options.why: The Pendleton Act covered only federal jobs. Urban machines such as Tammany Hall kept local patronage and stayed strong into the Progressive Era.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Political parties grew more dependent on contributions from wealthy businessmen and corporations
options.why: The law cut back the parties' ability to collect assessments from federal officeholders. As a result, national party organizations turned more and more to business donors for campaign money, as in the large corporate fundraising of 1896.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Political parties grew more dependent on contributions from wealthy businessmen and corporations". The law cut back the parties' ability to collect assessments from federal officeholders. As a result, national party organizations turned more and more to business donors for campaign money, as in the large corporate fundraising of 1896.
"Voter turnout in national elections fell sharply in the 1880s because patronage no longer drew partisans to the polls" is incorrect: Turnout in presidential elections stayed very high through the 1880s and 1890s. Strong party loyalty remained a defining feature of Gilded Age politics.
"Federal employees won the right to bargain collectively and to strike against the national government" is incorrect: The law set up merit hiring and protections, not collective bargaining. Federal workers gained no right to strike in this period.
"Party machines in large cities collapsed as municipal jobs became subject to federal competitive examinations" is incorrect: The Pendleton Act covered only federal jobs. Urban machines such as Tammany Hall kept local patronage and stayed strong into the Progressive Era.
facts: The Pendleton Act of 1883 barred the coercion of federal employees into making political contributions, which reduced the parties' reliance on officeholder assessments.
After the Pendleton Act, national parties relied more heavily on contributions from businesses and wealthy donors, as in the 1896 Republican campaign.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
Labor and Growth in the New South
Miriam Castellane, historian, Furnace and Furrow: Labor and Capital in the Georgia Piedmont, 1870-1900, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern academic monograph on Southern labor history)

"Boosters of the New South promised that railroads, cotton mills, and coal mines would free the region from its dependence on a single crop. Yet the labor arrangements behind this growth bound Black and poor white Southerners more tightly than the promoters admitted. In the cotton districts, sharecroppers who signed contracts each January pledged their share of the coming harvest to a furnishing merchant under the crop-lien system, and many ended the year owing more than when they began. In the mines, brickyards, and turpentine camps, states leased prisoners, most of them Black men convicted of vagrancy or petty theft, to private companies that paid the state a fee and housed them in brutal conditions. Industrial progress and agricultural debt, in short, were not opposites but partners. Both depended on workers who had little power to bargain, to move, or to refuse."

ush_set.theme: The New South, sharecropping and convict leasing
ush_set.title: Furnace and Furrow: Coerced Labor in the New South

sources.title: Labor and Growth in the New South
sources.attribution: Miriam Castellane, historian, Furnace and Furrow: Labor and Capital in the Georgia Piedmont, 1870-1900, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern academic monograph on Southern labor history)

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historian's main argument in the excerpt?

options.text: Economic growth in the New South depended on labor systems that sharply restricted workers' freedom.
options.why: The historian argues that industrial progress and agricultural debt were partners, both resting on workers with little power to bargain, move, or refuse, which matches the history of crop liens and convict leasing.
options.label: key

options.text: Sharecropping offered freedpeople a gradual path to landownership that industrial wage work in Southern cities could not provide.
options.why: The historian stresses that sharecroppers often sank deeper into debt, not that they moved toward owning land.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Convict leasing was chiefly a creation of Northern investors who used Southern prisons to evade the wage demands of organized labor.
options.why: The excerpt describes states leasing prisoners to private companies but makes no claim about Northern investors or union wage demands.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: Southern industrialization in the 1880s largely ended the region's reliance on cotton by drawing sharecroppers into mill and mine jobs.
options.why: The excerpt says boosters promised an end to single-crop dependence but that coercive arrangements persisted; cotton stayed dominant in much of the South.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Economic growth in the New South depended on labor systems that sharply restricted workers' freedom.". The historian argues that industrial progress and agricultural debt were partners, both resting on workers with little power to bargain, move, or refuse, which matches the history of crop liens and convict leasing.
"Sharecropping offered freedpeople a gradual path to landownership that industrial wage work in Southern cities could not provide." is incorrect: The historian stresses that sharecroppers often sank deeper into debt, not that they moved toward owning land.
"Convict leasing was chiefly a creation of Northern investors who used Southern prisons to evade the wage demands of organized labor." is incorrect: The excerpt describes states leasing prisoners to private companies but makes no claim about Northern investors or union wage demands.
"Southern industrialization in the 1880s largely ended the region's reliance on cotton by drawing sharecroppers into mill and mine jobs." is incorrect: The excerpt says boosters promised an end to single-crop dependence but that coercive arrangements persisted; cotton stayed dominant in much of the South.
facts: Under the crop-lien system after the Civil War, Southern tenants and sharecroppers pledged future crops to merchants for supplies on credit, often falling into debt.
Southern states leased convicts, disproportionately Black, to private companies in the late nineteenth century.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the historian's argument about workers in the New South?

options.text: The Supreme Court's 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson upholding a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black passengers
options.why: Plessy concerns legal segregation in public accommodations, not the labor arrangements of sharecropping and convict leasing.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: Southern laws after 1865 that punished vagrancy and allowed those unable to pay fines to be hired out
options.why: Vagrancy laws that turned unemployment into a crime and fed people into forced labor directly support the claim that workers had little power to refuse or move.
options.label: key

options.text: The founding of Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 to train Black students in agricultural and industrial trades
options.why: Tuskegee's founding concerns Black education and self-help, not evidence that workers were bound by debt or forced labor.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: The rapid expansion of railroad mileage across the former Confederate states during the 1880s, financed heavily by outside investors
options.why: Railroad growth is real and part of New South development, but it shows economic expansion, not the coercive labor conditions at the core of the argument.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Southern laws after 1865 that punished vagrancy and allowed those unable to pay fines to be hired out". Vagrancy laws that turned unemployment into a crime and fed people into forced labor directly support the claim that workers had little power to refuse or move.
"The Supreme Court's 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson upholding a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black passengers" is incorrect: Plessy concerns legal segregation in public accommodations, not the labor arrangements of sharecropping and convict leasing.
"The founding of Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 to train Black students in agricultural and industrial trades" is incorrect: Tuskegee's founding concerns Black education and self-help, not evidence that workers were bound by debt or forced labor.
"The rapid expansion of railroad mileage across the former Confederate states during the 1880s, financed heavily by outside investors" is incorrect: Railroad growth is real and part of New South development, but it shows economic expansion, not the coercive labor conditions at the core of the argument.
facts: Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865-1866 that included vagrancy laws allowing those unable to pay fines to be hired out.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars.

items.stem: The labor arrangements described in the excerpt expanded most directly in the context of which of the following?

options.text: The Populist Party's capture of Congress and the presidency on a platform of federal ownership of the railroads
options.why: The Populists called for government railroad ownership in 1892 but never won control of Congress or the presidency, and they challenged rather than created these conditions.
options.label: overstated

options.text: The Great Migration of Black Southerners to Northern industrial cities that left planters short of field laborers
options.why: The Great Migration began around World War I, well after these labor systems took hold in the 1870s and 1880s.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The return of Democratic Redeemer governments to power in Southern states as Reconstruction ended
options.why: Redeemer governments cut public spending, expanded convict leasing, and passed laws favoring landowners and merchants, providing the political setting for the systems in the excerpt.
options.label: key

options.text: The Freedmen's Bureau's widespread redistribution of confiscated plantation land to formerly enslaved families
options.why: Land redistribution largely failed; most confiscated land went back to former owners, which is why freedpeople turned to sharecropping.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The return of Democratic Redeemer governments to power in Southern states as Reconstruction ended". Redeemer governments cut public spending, expanded convict leasing, and passed laws favoring landowners and merchants, providing the political setting for the systems in the excerpt.
"The Populist Party's capture of Congress and the presidency on a platform of federal ownership of the railroads" is incorrect: The Populists called for government railroad ownership in 1892 but never won control of Congress or the presidency, and they challenged rather than created these conditions.
"The Great Migration of Black Southerners to Northern industrial cities that left planters short of field laborers" is incorrect: The Great Migration began around World War I, well after these labor systems took hold in the 1870s and 1880s.
"The Freedmen's Bureau's widespread redistribution of confiscated plantation land to formerly enslaved families" is incorrect: Land redistribution largely failed; most confiscated land went back to former owners, which is why freedpeople turned to sharecropping.
facts: Following the Compromise of 1877, federal troops were withdrawn from the South and Democratic 'Redeemer' governments controlled Southern states.
The Freedmen's Bureau did not carry out large-scale land redistribution; President Andrew Johnson returned most confiscated land to former owners in 1865.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why sharecropping became widespread in the South in the decades after the Civil War?

options.text: The Fifteenth Amendment required states to guarantee formerly enslaved people a share of the crops they raised.
options.why: The Fifteenth Amendment dealt with voting rights and said nothing about crop shares or labor contracts.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Large numbers of European immigrants settled in the rural South and demanded tenant contracts over wage labor.
options.why: Most European immigrants in this period went to Northern and Midwestern cities, not the rural South.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: The Homestead Act of 1862 moved most landless Southern farmers onto free federal land in the Great Plains.
options.why: Few landless Southerners, Black or white, got homesteads in the West; most stayed in the South as tenants and sharecroppers.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Freedpeople lacked land and capital, while landowners lacked cash to pay wages.
options.why: Sharecropping traded labor for a share of the crop, suiting landless freedpeople and cash-poor planters after emancipation and the war's destruction.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Freedpeople lacked land and capital, while landowners lacked cash to pay wages.". Sharecropping traded labor for a share of the crop, suiting landless freedpeople and cash-poor planters after emancipation and the war's destruction.
"The Fifteenth Amendment required states to guarantee formerly enslaved people a share of the crops they raised." is incorrect: The Fifteenth Amendment dealt with voting rights and said nothing about crop shares or labor contracts.
"Large numbers of European immigrants settled in the rural South and demanded tenant contracts over wage labor." is incorrect: Most European immigrants in this period went to Northern and Midwestern cities, not the rural South.
"The Homestead Act of 1862 moved most landless Southern farmers onto free federal land in the Great Plains." is incorrect: Few landless Southerners, Black or white, got homesteads in the West; most stayed in the South as tenants and sharecroppers.
facts: After the Civil War, most freedpeople did not receive land, and many planters had land but little cash, leading to sharecropping arrangements.
The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred denial of the vote on the basis of race and contained no economic guarantees.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
A historian on the local roots of Japanese American removal
Harriet Selwyn, historian, Fields and Fences: Farming, Race, and Removal in the Arroyo Verde Valley, 1900-1945, a study of a fictional California farming district, published 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a regional social history)

"When Army notices went up on telephone poles in the Arroyo Verde Valley in April 1942, ordering every person of Japanese ancestry to report for removal, the official reason was military necessity. Yet the orders landed in a district where Japanese farmers had been resented for thirty years. Issei growers there raised much of the valley's lettuce and strawberries, often on poor land they had made productive. California's Alien Land Law of 1913 had barred immigrants who could not become citizens from owning farmland, so many families held their acres in the names of their American-born children. In early 1942 a white growers' association from the valley sent a delegate to Washington to urge removal. A local editor wrote that the war gave the valley a chance to settle the Japanese question for good. Seen from Arroyo Verde, removal did not begin with Pearl Harbor. It finished a campaign that rival growers and nativist groups had waged for decades."

items.stem: Which of the following, if added to the excerpt, would most strengthen the author's argument about the causes of Japanese American removal?

It weakens her argument instead of strengthening it.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly modify the author's argument about why the removal of Japanese Americans occurred?

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the Supreme Court responded during the Second World War to a legal challenge to the exclusion orders described in the excerpt?

"The city papers say we in the hill counties are ignorant because our legislature has forbidden the teaching that man descended from a lower order of animals. The Petition and the Pamphlet
Thaddeus Reinholt, historian, Ballots Against the Bosses: Direct Democracy in the Pacific Northwest, 1898-1914, published 2019 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern political history of the Progressive Era)

"Oregon reformers after 1902 liked to describe the initiative and referendum as the people taking lawmaking back from a corrupt legislature, and that image has lasted. The record tells a more complicated story. The petitions that put measures on the ballot were circulated mostly by organized groups: the state Grange, a direct-legislation league, prohibitionists, and by 1910 paid canvassers working for business associations. In some elections voters received pamphlets describing more than two dozen measures, and many left the bottom of the ballot blank. Oregon practiced popular choice of senators years before the Seventeenth Amendment, but even that system depended on legislators keeping a pledge to follow the popular vote. Direct democracy did weaken the party machines and railroad lobbies that had dominated the statehouse. It did not abolish organized influence, however. It moved that influence out of the legislative cloakroom and into the petition drive and the campaign pamphlet."

Source A (secondary source)
A National Audience
Harriet Ellery Voss, historian, Signals and Highways: Making a National Market, 1919-1932, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a cultural history of American consumerism)

"Between 1919 and 1929 the radio set and the motorcar did more to knit Americans into a single audience than any statute or sermon. Once broadcasters linked stations into coast-to-coast networks in the late 1920s, a family in rural Nebraska could hear the same dance band, ballgame, and soap advertisement as a family in Philadelphia. The Model T, its price cut again and again by the moving assembly line, carried farm families to town movie houses and chain stores. Installment plans let a clerk drive a car he could never have bought outright. Advertisers, sensing the new audience, sold not only goods but a common picture of the good life. Regional isolation gave way to a national marketplace of tastes."

———

Source B (secondary source)
Prosperity on Credit
Daniel Okoro Brandt, historian, The Mortgaged Decade: Farms, Factories, and Debt in the 1920s, 2016 (ALTON-composed, in the style of an economic and social history of the interwar years)

"Celebrations of a consumer republic in the 1920s tend to describe the view from a city apartment. Most farm households still lacked electric power at the decade's end, and many listened to battery radios, if they owned radios at all. Crop prices had collapsed after the wartime boom, so farm families who bought cars often bought them on credit they struggled to repay. In industrial towns, wages lagged behind the output of the factories, and installment debt filled the gap between what workers earned and what manufacturers needed to sell. The new goods were real, but the prosperity that carried them rested on borrowed money and was spread far more narrowly than the advertisements suggested."

"We broke out the last of the buffalo grass on our north quarter in 1919, when wheat brought better than two dollars a bushel and the government told us wheat would win the war. My husband mortgaged the place to buy a tractor and a one-way plow, and for some years the crops paid. Now wheat will not fetch thirty cents at the elevator, and the tractor note comes due just the same. The Farmers State Bank closed its doors in November with our savings inside. Since February the wind has not let up for more than four days together. Dirt sifts under the doors and lies in drifts along the fence rows, and the seed we drilled last fall is blown clean out of the ground. items.stem: The conditions described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments later in the 1930s?

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(secondary source)
A historian on the Open Door notes
Eleanor Strand Whitcomb, An Empire of Access: Americans and the China Market, 1895-1925, from a lecture series published by the fictional Harlow College Press, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic historian's interpretive survey)

"When Secretary of State John Hay sent out his Open Door notes in 1899, he was not rejecting empire so much as redefining it. American manufacturers, especially the cotton mills of the Carolinas and New England, pictured China's four hundred million people as buyers of American cloth and kerosene. Yet the United States held no sphere of its own on the Chinese coast, and few in Congress wanted to pay for one. Hay's answer was an empire of access: equal tariffs and harbor rights for every foreign trader, protected not by garrisons but by the mutual suspicion of the great powers. The policy was cheap, and that was its appeal. It was also fragile. For two decades Washington defended the principle chiefly with notes, conferences, and treaties, trusting that rival powers would honor in China a restraint they would never have accepted at home."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument about the Open Door policy?

options.text: It sought commercial access to China without the costs of holding colonies there.

options.text: It marked an American turn toward seizing Chinese ports to match the spheres that European powers held.
options.why: The author stresses that the United States held no sphere and chose access over territorial control, the opposite of seizing ports.
options.label: reversal

options.text: It grew mainly out of Protestant missionary demands that Washington protect converts and mission schools in the Chinese interior.
options.why: Missionaries were active in China, but the excerpt traces the policy to manufacturers' hopes for markets, not missionary pressure.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: It successfully abolished the foreign spheres of influence in China and restored full Chinese control over tariffs.
options.why: The author calls the policy fragile and dependent on rivals' restraint; the spheres of influence were not abolished.
options.label: overstated

options.text: A Populist campaign for free coinage of silver to relieve indebted farmers in the South and on the Great Plains

options.text: A drive by business and political leaders to find overseas markets after the depression of 1893

options.label: key

options.text: A broad revival of the anti-imperialist movement that blocked the annexation of overseas territories after 1898

options.label: reversal

items.stem: The commitment to the Open Door described in the excerpt contributed most directly to which development in the period from 1931 to 1941?

options.text: Adoption of the Good Neighbor policy, which renounced armed intervention in the internal affairs of Latin American nations
options.why: The Good Neighbor policy concerned Latin America and did not grow out of the Open Door in China.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Passage of the Neutrality Acts, which barred loans and arms sales to nations at war in order to keep the country out of conflict

"Passage of the Neutrality Acts, which barred loans and arms sales to nations at war in order to keep the country out of conflict" is incorrect: The Neutrality Acts came from disillusionment with World War I and fears about Europe, not from the commitment to trade access in China.

items.stem: The campaign described in the excerpt is best understood as part of which broader context of the early twentieth century?

items.stem: After the change urged in the excerpt was achieved in 1920, some suffrage activists most directly continued their efforts by doing which of the following?

options.text: Demanding that the Fifteenth Amendment be revised to ban voting discrimination based on sex as well as race
options.why: Debate over excluding sex from the Fifteenth Amendment split suffragists around 1869, not after 1920.

options.text: Pressing Congress to pass the Equal Pay Act requiring employers to pay men and women the same wages for the same work
options.why: The Equal Pay Act was a 1963 achievement of a later era of women's activism.
options.label: wrong_period

options.why: The National Woman's Party, led by veterans of the suffrage campaign, introduced the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 to extend legal equality beyond the vote.

Economic Aid and Early Containment
Corinne Albrecht, Ledgers and Rifles: American Aid and the Remaking of Western Europe, 1947-1952, a university press monograph, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a diplomatic history monograph)

"Historians who picture the early Cold War as a contest of tanks and bombers miss how the Truman administration first chose to fight it. When the president asked Congress in March 1947 for aid to Greece and Turkey, he described the struggle as a choice between two ways of life. Even so, he asked for dollars and advisers, not American combat troops. The European Recovery Program, approved the following year, carried that logic further. State Department planners reasoned that hungry, unemployed voters in France and Italy, where communist parties polled strongly, were the Kremlin's best allies. Grain, coal, and machine tools, they believed, would do more than divisions of soldiers to keep western Europe out of Soviet hands. The aid also came with conditions. Recipients had to coordinate their recovery plans and lower barriers to trade, which tied them to one another and to the United States. Until 1950, containment was a wager that ledgers could accomplish what rifles could not."

items.stem: Which of the following was most likely a result of the European Recovery Program described in the excerpt?

options.text: It persuaded the Soviet Union to permit free elections in Poland and other eastern European nations in return for American loans.

options.text: It allowed the United States to withdraw nearly all of its military forces from western Europe by the early 1950s.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
(primary source)
Statement to a county board of commissioners, central Pennsylvania, January 1974
Statement of Delia Marchetti, owner of the Crossroads Grill on Route 22, to a county board of commissioners' hearing on local economic conditions, January 1974 (ALTON-composed, in the style of public testimony at a local hearing during the 1973-1974 oil embargo)

"I have run the Crossroads Grill on Route 22 for nineteen years, and I have never seen a winter like this one. Since the Arab oil countries cut off shipments in October, the truckers who were my bread and butter sit in gas lines in Harrisburg instead of at my counter. The new 55-mile limit and the Sunday station closings keep the tourists at home. Meanwhile everything I buy costs more: coffee, beef, the heating oil for the dining room. I have raised the price of a hamburger twice since summer and still lost money in December. My cook's husband was laid off at the steel fabricating plant, so she asked for a raise I cannot give her. They tell us on television that prices climb when business is booming and fall when business is slow. Then somebody in Washington should explain why we have both troubles at once. I ask this board to press our congressman for fuel allocation rules that remember small businesses, not only the big oil companies."

ush_set.title: A Roadside Diner Owner Confronts the 1973-1974 Oil Embargo

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Marchetti's point of view in the excerpt?

options.text: A small business owner seeking federal fuel policies that protect independent firms like hers
options.why: Marchetti describes her own diner's losses and closes by asking the board to press for fuel allocation rules that remember small businesses, not only big oil companies.
options.label: key

options.text: An environmental activist praising the speed limit and station closings as needed steps toward reducing air pollution
options.why: She mentions the 55-mile limit and Sunday closings only as reasons tourists stay home, not as environmental gains.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: An oil company spokesperson arguing that higher fuel prices were needed to encourage new domestic drilling and exploration
options.why: Marchetti contrasts small businesses with the big oil companies and complains about rising costs; she does not defend higher prices.
options.label: reversal

options.text: A union organizer demanding that employers raise wages for workers to keep pace with the rising cost of living
options.why: She is an employer who says she cannot give her cook a raise; the wage request comes from her employee, not from her.

items.stem: Marchetti supports her claim that the economy had 'both troubles at once' mainly by pointing to which of the following?

options.text: Soaring profits reported by the major oil companies during the months after the embargo began
options.why: She mentions big oil companies only in her policy request and cites no profit figures.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: Rising prices for her supplies alongside a local layoff and fewer customers
options.why: She pairs higher costs for coffee, beef, and heating oil with lost trucker and tourist business and her cook's husband's layoff, showing rising prices during a slowdown.
options.label: key

options.text: Tourists trading in large automobiles for smaller and more fuel-efficient imported cars
options.why: The shift toward smaller imported cars was real in the 1970s, but the excerpt says only that tourists stay home.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: Her decision to grant her cook a raise to keep pace with the rising cost of food and fuel

items.stem: The economic hardships Marchetti describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: The postwar Marshall Plan, which shifted American petroleum supplies toward the rebuilding of Western European industry

options.text: The 1979 Iranian Revolution, which disrupted Middle Eastern oil exports and produced a second round of gasoline shortages
options.why: The excerpt is dated January 1974 and refers to the cutoff that began in October 1973, years before the 1979 crisis.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Growing U.S. reliance on imported oil, exposed when Arab OPEC states imposed an embargo in 1973
options.why: By the early 1970s the United States imported a large share of its oil. The embargo, imposed in response to U.S. support for Israel in the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, caused the shortages and price increases she describes.
options.label: key

options.text: Federal deregulation of the trucking and airline industries, which lowered freight rates and pressured small roadside firms
options.why: Airline and trucking deregulation came in 1978 and 1980, after this testimony, and it is not what she blames.
options.label: wrong_period

The correct answer is "Growing U.S. reliance on imported oil, exposed when Arab OPEC states imposed an embargo in 1973". By the early 1970s the United States imported a large share of its oil. "The postwar Marshall Plan, which shifted American petroleum supplies toward the rebuilding of Western European industry" is incorrect: The Marshall Plan (1948-1952) was economic aid to postwar Europe and has nothing to do with the fuel shortages of 1973-1974.
"The 1979 Iranian Revolution, which disrupted Middle Eastern oil exports and produced a second round of gasoline shortages" is incorrect: The excerpt is dated January 1974 and refers to the cutoff that began in October 1973, years before the 1979 crisis.
"Federal deregulation of the trucking and airline industries, which lowered freight rates and pressured small roadside firms" is incorrect: Airline and trucking deregulation came in 1978 and 1980, after this testimony, and it is not what she blames.
facts: The 1973 Arab oil embargo was a response to U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Arab-Israeli (Yom Kippur) War.

items.stem: The combination of economic problems Marchetti describes is best identified as which of the following developments of the 1970s?

options.text: Deflation, in which falling prices and wages squeezed debtors much as they had in the early 1930s
options.why: She describes rising prices, not falling ones. Deflation marked the Great Depression, not the 1970s.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Supply-side recovery, in which tax cuts spurred investment and business expansion across the country
options.why: Supply-side policies are tied to the Reagan administration in the 1980s, which came after and partly in response to stagflation.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: An economic boom driven by consumer credit, suburban home building, and federal highway spending
options.why: This describes postwar prosperity in the 1950s and 1960s, not the slump in the excerpt.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Stagflation, in which high inflation coincided with slow growth and rising unemployment
options.why: She describes prices climbing while business slows and workers lose jobs. That pairing defined stagflation in the 1970s and undercut the usual assumption that inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Stagflation, in which high inflation coincided with slow growth and rising unemployment". She describes prices climbing while business slows and workers lose jobs. That pairing defined stagflation in the 1970s and undercut the usual assumption that inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions.
"Deflation, in which falling prices and wages squeezed debtors much as they had in the early 1930s" is incorrect: She describes rising prices, not falling ones. Deflation marked the Great Depression, not the 1970s.
"Supply-side recovery, in which tax cuts spurred investment and business expansion across the country" is incorrect: Supply-side policies are tied to the Reagan administration in the 1980s, which came after and partly in response to stagflation.
"An economic boom driven by consumer credit, suburban home building, and federal highway spending" is incorrect: This describes postwar prosperity in the 1950s and 1960s, not the slump in the excerpt.
facts: Stagflation, inflation combined with economic stagnation and high unemployment, marked the U.S. economy in the 1970s.
Supply-side tax cuts were a centerpiece of Reagan administration policy beginning in 1981.

payload.set_intro:

(secondary source)
A historian on GI Bill housing benefits in postwar Ohio
Dorothea Lindqvist, historian, Paper Deeds: Veterans, Mortgages, and the Making of a Suburban County, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historian's monograph; author, book, and development are fictional)

"Historians often call the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 a ladder into the middle class. In the tract developments that went up outside Cleveland after 1946, though, the ladder was missing rungs. The law's loan guarantees let a veteran buy a two-bedroom house in a place like Brookfield Acres with little or no down payment, and the monthly payments often came to less than city rents. Yet the act left approval to local banks and Veterans Administration offices. Those offices followed Federal Housing Administration appraisal rules that rated mixed or Black neighborhoods as poor risks, and builders wrote racial restrictions into their sales contracts. Of the first 3,100 VA-backed mortgages recorded in the county, fewer than 40 went to Black veterans. So the suburbs that federal money built were more than a reward for service. They came out of policy choices that turned equal wartime sacrifice into unequal postwar wealth."

items.stem: Which of the following findings, if documented, would most weaken the author's argument about postwar suburban housing?

items.stem: The rapid construction of housing developments like the one described in the excerpt after 1946 was most directly a response to which of the following?

options.text: New Deal public housing programs that had already moved most urban working families into federally owned apartments
options.why: New Deal public housing existed but housed only a small share of urban families. It did not satisfy demand or set off the suburban boom.

options.text: Wartime price controls and rationing that were extended into the 1950s to restrain consumer demand for durable goods

Civil Defense Bulletin to the Households of Calder Springs
Bulletin issued by Walter Brandt, civil defense director of Calder Springs, a fictional town in southern Georgia, October 24, 1962 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a local civil defense bulletin)

"To the Households of Calder Springs: On Monday evening the President told the nation that Soviet offensive missiles are being installed in Cuba, scarcely ninety miles from our coast, and that our Navy will stop any ship carrying such weapons to the island. Our town lies well within the reach of these missiles. I do not write to frighten you but to ask you to act. Every family should store two weeks of canned food and water in a cellar or in the inner room farthest from windows. The basement of the First Methodist Church and the county courthouse have been stocked as public fallout shelters, and the yellow and black signs are now posted. Schoolchildren will continue the drills they have practiced since spring. The President has chosen firmness over surrender, and the strength of the nation rests on calm, prepared citizens at home as much as on ships at sea. Keep your radio tuned to the civil defense frequencies marked on the dial, and do not crowd the telephone lines."

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the crisis described in the bulletin was resolved later in 1962?

options.text: American forces invaded Cuba, destroyed the missile sites, and removed Fidel Castro's government from power
options.why: The United States never invaded Cuba during the crisis, and Castro stayed in power for decades.

options.text: The United States agreed to withdraw all of its troops and nuclear weapons from its NATO allies in Western Europe
options.why: The United States only privately agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey; American forces stayed in Western Europe.
options.label: overstated

options.text: The Soviet Union removed its missiles from Cuba after the United States pledged not to invade the island

(secondary source)
Watergate and the Decade of Doubt
Corinne Haldane, historian, from The Broken Covenant: Americans and Their Government, 1964-1980, a lecture series delivered at a public university in Sacramento, California, 2009 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian's interpretive study of postwar political culture)

"It is tempting to treat Watergate as the moment Americans stopped believing their leaders, but the scandal is better understood as a confirmation than a cause. By 1968, the distance between official optimism about Vietnam and the scenes on the evening news had already earned its own label among reporters: the credibility gap. The publication of the Pentagon Papers in 1971 showed that several administrations, Democratic and Republican alike, had misled the public about the war's course and prospects. What Watergate added was proof that deception reached into domestic politics and into the Oval Office itself. The White House tapes, released after the Supreme Court ruled against the president in 1974, turned private suspicion into documented fact. Congressional investigations of the intelligence agencies the following year deepened the damage. Watergate, in short, gave a name and a face to a distrust that had been a decade in the making."

Testimony of Ruth Ellen Dvorak, a drill press operator at a valve plant and member of a machinists' union local, before a ratification hearing of a Midwestern state legislature, 1973 (ALTON-composed, in the style of public hearing testimony on the Equal Rights Amendment)

"I have run a drill press at the Hollis Valve plant in Marlow County for eleven years. Last spring the company posted an opening for a setup man, paying forty cents more an hour. I was told I could not bid on it, because the law of this state says a woman may not lift more than twenty-five pounds or work more than nine hours in a day. They call these laws protection. I call them a fence. The men on my line lift what I lift, and they get the overtime and the promotions. The Congress sent you this amendment last year by a wide margin, and all it says is that equality of rights under the law shall not be denied on account of sex. Some ladies have come before you to warn that it will draft our daughters and end a wife's claim to support. I am a wife and a mother myself, and I ask you this: what support is there in a paycheck made smaller because of who I am?"

A historian on postwar Mexican American and Native activism
Marisol Etcheverry, historian, from Claiming the Ground: Mexican American and Native Activism in the Postwar West, a book based on her lectures at a university in Albuquerque, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a modern historical monograph)

"Between the late 1940s and the early 1970s, Mexican American and American Indian activists moved away from a politics that asked for inclusion on the majority's terms and toward one that demanded control over their own communities. Earlier organizations such as the American GI Forum, founded by Mexican American veterans in 1948, had stressed citizenship, patriotism, and legal equality. By 1968, students walking out of East Los Angeles high schools were demanding bilingual instruction and teachers who knew their history, while the American Indian Movement was organizing in Minneapolis. The nineteen-month occupation of Alcatraz Island that began in 1969 cast Native claims in the language of treaty rights and nationhood rather than integration. What linked these campaigns was less a shared program than a shared conviction that cultural identity was a source of political power, not an obstacle to be shed."

items.stem: The Native American activism described in the excerpt was most directly a reaction against which federal policy of the 1950s?

"The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924, which granted United States citizenship to all Native Americans born in the country" is incorrect: The citizenship act came in the 1920s, not the 1950s, and it was not the federal policy that prompted the demands of the late 1960s.

"Friends, for forty years this valley built the airplanes and missile guidance systems that kept the Soviets in check. When the President called for a stronger defense ten years ago, our payrolls doubled, and a machinist with a high school diploma could buy a house on Las Palmas Avenue. Last month the red flag came down over the Kremlin. I rejoice in that as much as anyone here; my father flew in Korea. But I would be failing you if I pretended that peace is free for Vista Arroyo. Congress is already talking about a peace dividend, and Washington will not keep buying bombers to fight an enemy that no longer exists. Halvorsen Aerospace has announced 1,800 layoffs. We cannot wait for the Pentagon to rescue us. I am asking every bank and business in this room to help us court new industries: commercial electronics, medical equipment, and trade with the nations of the Pacific."

payload.set_intro:
ALTON-composed stimulus
Source A (secondary source)
Excerpt A: A historian on the Contract's lasting influence
Corinne Haldane, The Hundred Days That Lasted: Congress and the Conservative Turn, 2011 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a political historian of the late twentieth century)

"When House Republicans unveiled their Contract with America on the Capitol steps in September 1994, many commentators dismissed it as campaign theater. They were mistaken. That November, voters gave Republicans control of both chambers of Congress, and the new House majority was the party's first in forty years. During the first hundred days of 1995, the House voted on every item in the Contract. More important, the document changed the terms of national debate. A Democratic president who had campaigned on an active federal government soon found himself bargaining over how quickly, not whether, to balance the federal budget. The Contract did not need to become law in its entirety to succeed. It moved the political center of gravity decisively to the right, and that shift outlasted the men who drafted it."

———

Source B (secondary source)
Excerpt B: A historian on the limits of the Republican Revolution
Theodore Okafor-Lind, Gridlock and Bargain: Divided Government in the Clinton Years, 2015 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a historian of American political institutions)

"People often remember the Republican landslide of 1994 as a revolution, but its legislative record was thinner than its rhetoric. A constitutional amendment imposing congressional term limits failed in the House, and the balanced budget amendment fell short in the Senate. When Speaker Newt Gingrich's majority clashed with the White House over spending in the winter of 1995 to 1996, two partial shutdowns of the federal government followed, and most voters blamed congressional Republicans. Bill Clinton won reelection comfortably the next year. What emerged was less a conservative triumph than an uneasy bargaining relationship. Each side claimed credit for compromises neither had wanted, and partisan distrust in Washington deepened with every round."

The correct answer is "The 1980s conservative effort under Reagan to cut taxes, reduce regulation, and shrink federal social spending". The Contract's calls for balanced budgets, tax cuts, and a smaller federal government carried forward the conservative program of the Reagan years, including the 1981 tax cuts and deregulation.
"The Great Society's commitment to using federal funds and new agencies to fight poverty and expand access to health coverage" is incorrect: The Contract tried to roll back federal social programs of the kind the Great Society created, such as Medicaid and the antipoverty programs, not extend them.
"The Progressive Era campaign to build federal regulatory agencies that would police large corporations and protect consumers from fraud" is incorrect: The Contract aimed to reduce federal regulation, while Progressives worked to expand it.
"The New Deal coalition's support for federal labor protections, large public works programs, and a strong political role for unions" is incorrect: The Contract opposed the activist federal government that the New Deal coalition stood for.
facts: Ronald Reagan signed major income tax cuts in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 and pursued deregulation in the 1980s.
The Contract with America (1994) called for a balanced budget amendment, tax cuts, and reductions in the size of the federal government.

ALTON-composed stimulus
(primary source)
Remarks at a Community Forum on the War in the Persian Gulf
Remarks by Walter Brannigan, a Vietnam veteran and member of the Corbin County school board, at a community forum held in the Millersport High School gymnasium, Millersport, Missouri, February 1991 (ALTON-composed, in the style of a local public speech)

"I stood in this gymnasium in 1968 and argued with my own father about a war neither of us understood. Tonight I want to tell you why this one feels different to me. When Iraq's army rolled into Kuwait last August, the President did not act alone. The United Nations set a deadline, and nations from Britain to Egypt to Saudi Arabia sent forces. Congress debated and voted before the bombing began, which is more than it did in my war. Even the Soviets, who once would have blocked anything we proposed, stood aside. I am not naive. Oil is part of this, and so is pride. Some of our generals want to bury the memory of Saigon for good. But our sons and daughters over there have a mission they can name: push Iraq out of Kuwait and come home. So tie your yellow ribbons, and keep your questions sharp."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Brannigan's point of view in the excerpt?

options.text: He backs the war mainly because it has international and congressional support that Vietnam lacked.
options.why: Brannigan contrasts the UN deadline, the multinational coalition, and the congressional vote with his own war in Vietnam, which was never formally declared or debated in the same way.
options.label: key

options.text: He supports the war as a necessary step toward overthrowing the Iraqi government and occupying Baghdad indefinitely.
options.why: He describes the mission as expelling Iraq from Kuwait and coming home, not regime change or occupation.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: He opposes the war because he believes it is being fought chiefly to protect American access to Persian Gulf oil.
options.why: He admits oil is a factor but asks listeners to support the troops; he does not oppose the war.
options.label: reversal

options.text: He favors the war as a continuation of the containment policy aimed at checking Soviet influence in the Middle East.
options.why: He notes that the Soviets stood aside; he does not present the war as a fight against Soviet influence.
options.label: misattributed

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "He backs the war mainly because it has international and congressional support that Vietnam lacked.". Brannigan contrasts the UN deadline, the multinational coalition, and the congressional vote with his own war in Vietnam, which was never formally declared or debated in the same way.
"He supports the war as a necessary step toward overthrowing the Iraqi government and occupying Baghdad indefinitely." is incorrect: He describes the mission as expelling Iraq from Kuwait and coming home, not regime change or occupation.
"He opposes the war because he believes it is being fought chiefly to protect American access to Persian Gulf oil." is incorrect: He admits oil is a factor but asks listeners to support the troops; he does not oppose the war.
"He favors the war as a continuation of the containment policy aimed at checking Soviet influence in the Middle East." is incorrect: He notes that the Soviets stood aside; he does not present the war as a fight against Soviet influence.
facts: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990.
The UN Security Council authorized force against Iraq if it did not leave Kuwait by January 15, 1991, and Congress voted to authorize force in January 1991.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Brannigan's claim that American forces had a limited mission they "can name"?

options.text: In 2003 American forces invaded Iraq, removed Saddam Hussein from power, and began a lengthy occupation of the country.
options.why: The 2003 Iraq War was a separate, later conflict and points to a broader commitment, not the limited 1991 mission.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Coalition forces ended the ground campaign once Iraqi troops had been driven out of Kuwait.
options.why: The ceasefire after Kuwait was liberated, without a march on Baghdad, matches the limited goal Brannigan describes.
options.label: key

options.text: Retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells on fire, creating a severe environmental disaster in the region.
options.why: The oil well fires did happen, but they say nothing about whether the American mission stayed limited.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: American aircraft patrolled no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq for more than a decade after the fighting.
options.why: The long-running no-fly zones show an ongoing commitment, which would weaken his claim that troops would simply come home.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Coalition forces ended the ground campaign once Iraqi troops had been driven out of Kuwait.". The ceasefire after Kuwait was liberated, without a march on Baghdad, matches the limited goal Brannigan describes.
"In 2003 American forces invaded Iraq, removed Saddam Hussein from power, and began a lengthy occupation of the country." is incorrect: The 2003 Iraq War was a separate, later conflict and points to a broader commitment, not the limited 1991 mission.
"Retreating Iraqi troops set hundreds of Kuwaiti oil wells on fire, creating a severe environmental disaster in the region." is incorrect: The oil well fires did happen, but they say nothing about whether the American mission stayed limited.
"American aircraft patrolled no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq for more than a decade after the fighting." is incorrect: The long-running no-fly zones show an ongoing commitment, which would weaken his claim that troops would simply come home.
facts: The coalition ground offensive in Operation Desert Storm lasted about one hundred hours, and a ceasefire took effect at the end of February 1991 after Iraqi forces were expelled from Kuwait.
Saddam Hussein remained in power after the 1991 war.

items.stem: Brannigan's remark that the Soviets "stood aside" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: The Soviet Union had already dissolved into independent republics, leaving Russia too weak to oppose American policy.
options.why: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, after the Gulf War had ended.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Nixon's policy of détente had produced arms limitation treaties and expanded trade between the superpowers in the 1970s.
options.why: Détente in the 1970s gave way to renewed tension around 1980 and does not explain Soviet behavior in 1990 and 1991.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Gorbachev's reforms and the 1989 fall of Eastern European communist regimes had eased superpower rivalry.
options.why: As the Cold War wound down, the Soviet Union did not use its Security Council veto against action on Iraq, which made the coalition possible.
options.label: key

options.text: The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan had freed Soviet troops to join the coalition forces assembling in Saudi Arabia.
options.why: The Soviets did leave Afghanistan by 1989, but they did not send troops to fight with the coalition.
options.label: overstated

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Gorbachev's reforms and the 1989 fall of Eastern European communist regimes had eased superpower rivalry.". As the Cold War wound down, the Soviet Union did not use its Security Council veto against action on Iraq, which made the coalition possible.
"The Soviet Union had already dissolved into independent republics, leaving Russia too weak to oppose American policy." is incorrect: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, after the Gulf War had ended.
"Nixon's policy of détente had produced arms limitation treaties and expanded trade between the superpowers in the 1970s." is incorrect: Détente in the 1970s gave way to renewed tension around 1980 and does not explain Soviet behavior in 1990 and 1991.
"The Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan had freed Soviet troops to join the coalition forces assembling in Saudi Arabia." is incorrect: The Soviets did leave Afghanistan by 1989, but they did not send troops to fight with the coalition.
facts: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost and perestroika began in the mid-1980s.
Communist governments in Eastern Europe fell in 1989, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

items.stem: Brannigan's comment that some generals wanted to "bury the memory of Saigon" relates most directly to which effect of the Persian Gulf War?

options.text: Congress responded by passing the War Powers Resolution, requiring presidents to consult lawmakers before sending troops into combat.
options.why: The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 as a reaction to Vietnam, not to the Gulf War.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The war's outcome led the United States to withdraw its forces from the Persian Gulf and sharply reduce its reliance on imported oil.
options.why: After the war the United States kept a larger military presence in the Gulf, and oil imports remained high.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Public anger over high casualties produced a large antiwar movement that forced Congress to cut the defense budget.
options.why: American casualties were low and the war was popular. Later defense cuts came from the end of the Cold War, not from an antiwar movement.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Quick victory revived confidence in American military power and eased post-Vietnam reluctance to intervene.
options.why: The fast, low-casualty victory raised public trust in the military and made Americans less wary of using force abroad, a wariness that dated to defeat in Vietnam.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Quick victory revived confidence in American military power and eased post-Vietnam reluctance to intervene.". The fast, low-casualty victory raised public trust in the military and made Americans less wary of using force abroad, a wariness that dated to defeat in Vietnam.
"Congress responded by passing the War Powers Resolution, requiring presidents to consult lawmakers before sending troops into combat." is incorrect: The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 as a reaction to Vietnam, not to the Gulf War.
"The war's outcome led the United States to withdraw its forces from the Persian Gulf and sharply reduce its reliance on imported oil." is incorrect: After the war the United States kept a larger military presence in the Gulf, and oil imports remained high.
"Public anger over high casualties produced a large antiwar movement that forced Congress to cut the defense budget." is incorrect: American casualties were low and the war was popular. Later defense cuts came from the end of the Cold War, not from an antiwar movement.
facts: The Persian Gulf War ended in a quick coalition victory in February 1991 with relatively few American casualties.
The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973, during the final years of the Vietnam War.
